cardiac-cycle.name: The cardiac cycle
cardiac-cycle.summary: One heartbeat is a sequence of filling and ejection: diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill, and systole, when they contract and pump.
body: Each cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds at rest. During diastole the mitral and tricuspid valves are open and blood flows passively from the atria into the ventricles; the atria then contract to add the final fifth. Ventricular systole begins as pressure rises, the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut (the first heart sound, 'lub'), and once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure the aortic and pulmonary valves open and blood is ejected.

As the ventricles relax, pressure falls, the aortic and pulmonary valves close (the second heart sound, 'dub') and the cycle repeats. The valves make flow one-way; the papillary muscles and chordae tendineae stop the mitral and tricuspid leaflets bulging back into the atria.
The fraction of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected, the ejection fraction, is normally 55 to 70% and is the everyday measure of how well the left ventricle pumps.

heart-rate.name: Heart rate
heart-rate.summary: How often the heart beats, set by the sinoatrial node and adjusted second by second by the autonomic nervous system and hormones.
body: The sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium fires spontaneously about 100 times a minute if left alone. At rest the vagus nerve slows it to a typical 60 to 100 beats per minute; sympathetic nerves and adrenaline speed it up during exercise, fear or fever.

Trained athletes often have resting rates in the 40s because each beat pumps more blood. Rates persistently above 100 (tachycardia) or below 60 (bradycardia) are only abnormal in context: a rate of 45 in a marathon runner is normal, in a fainting older adult it may signal heart block.
Heart rate is one of the vital signs and is measured at the radial pulse, on an ECG, or by pulse oximeters and wearables.

blood-pressure.name: Blood pressure
blood-pressure.summary: The pressure blood exerts on artery walls: systolic at the peak of ejection, diastolic between beats.
body: Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps each minute (cardiac output) and how hard it is to push that blood through the small arteries (peripheral resistance). The elastic aorta smooths the pulse; the muscular arterioles set resistance and are the main site of control.

Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch report pressure to the brainstem, which adjusts heart rate and vessel tone within seconds. Over hours and days the kidneys take over, adjusting salt and water excretion through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic in millimetres of mercury. Values around 120/80 mmHg are typical; sustained readings of 140/90 mmHg or more define hypertension in most guidelines.

cardiac-output.name: Cardiac output
cardiac-output.summary: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, about five litres at rest.
body: Stroke volume, the amount ejected per beat, rises when the ventricle fills more (the Frank-Starling mechanism: a more stretched muscle contracts harder), when contractility increases under sympathetic drive, and when the resistance it pumps against falls.

During hard exercise cardiac output can reach 20 to 25 litres per minute in a fit adult, mostly through a faster rate and a larger stroke volume, while blood is redirected from the gut and kidneys to the muscles.
A failing heart cannot raise its output to meet demand; the resulting breathlessness on exertion and fluid retention are the hallmarks of heart failure.

cardiac-conduction.name: Electrical conduction of the heart
cardiac-conduction.summary: A wiring system of specialised muscle cells spreads each heartbeat from the sinoatrial node through the atria, the atrioventricular node and the bundle branches to the ventricles.
body: The impulse starts in the sinoatrial node, sweeps across both atria (the P wave of the ECG) and reaches the atrioventricular node, which delays it for about a tenth of a second so the atria finish emptying. It then races down the bundle of His and the right and left bundle branches to the Purkinje fibres, depolarising the ventricles from the apex upward (the QRS complex). Recovery of the ventricles produces the T wave.

Because the wave follows a fixed path, its timing on an ECG reveals blocks (a long PR interval or a bundle branch block), extra pathways and the chaotic atrial activity of atrial fibrillation. Damaged muscle after a heart attack changes the shape of the QRS and ST segments.
Pacemakers replace a failing sinoatrial node or a blocked atrioventricular node; ablation destroys tissue that generates abnormal rhythms.

circulation.name: Circulation
circulation.summary: Two circuits in series: the pulmonary circulation loads blood with oxygen in the lungs, the systemic circulation delivers it to every organ.
body: The right heart pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary arteries into the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and unloads carbon dioxide before returning through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The left heart pumps it into the aorta and on through arteries, arterioles and capillaries, where exchange with the tissues happens, then back through venules and veins to the right atrium.

Pressure falls along the way: from about 120 mmHg in the aorta to a few mmHg in the great veins. Veins hold about two thirds of the blood volume at any moment and return it to the heart with the help of valves, the muscle pump of the legs and the suction of breathing.
Special circuits exist: the hepatic portal system carries gut blood through the liver first, and the coronary circulation supplies the heart muscle itself during diastole.

breathing.name: Breathing (ventilation)
breathing.summary: Air moves in and out because muscles change the volume of the chest: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge it for inspiration; relaxation and elastic recoil empty it.
body: When the diaphragm contracts its dome flattens and the ribs swing up and out, lowering pressure inside the chest below atmospheric pressure so air flows in. Quiet expiration is passive: the stretched lungs and chest wall recoil. Forced breathing recruits the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals to push air out, and the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids to pull the ribs up.

The rhythm is generated in the medulla and pons and adjusted by chemoreceptors that sense carbon dioxide and, to a lesser extent, oxygen. A rising carbon dioxide level is the strongest normal drive to breathe.
Airway resistance matters: narrowing the bronchi even slightly, as in asthma, greatly increases the work of breathing because resistance rises with the fourth power of the reduction in radius.

gas-exchange.name: Gas exchange
gas-exchange.summary: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin wall between alveoli and capillaries by diffusion, driven by differences in partial pressure.
body: The lungs contain about 300 million alveoli with a combined surface close to the size of a tennis court, separated from blood by a membrane under a micrometre thick. Oxygen diffuses into the blood because its partial pressure in alveolar air (about 100 mmHg) exceeds that in returning venous blood (about 40 mmHg); carbon dioxide moves the other way down a smaller gradient because it diffuses twenty times more readily.

Efficient exchange needs ventilation and blood flow to be matched. Blood sent to unventilated alveoli (as in pneumonia) is not oxygenated, and ventilated alveoli without blood flow (as in pulmonary embolism) are wasted breath. The lungs partly correct this by constricting vessels in poorly ventilated regions.
Thickening of the membrane (fibrosis) or fluid in the alveoli (pulmonary oedema) slows diffusion, and oxygen, with its lower solubility, is affected first.

oxygen-transport.name: Oxygen transport
oxygen-transport.summary: Almost all oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin in red cells; how tightly it binds changes with the tissue's needs.
body: Each haemoglobin molecule carries four oxygen molecules, and a litre of arterial blood holds about 200 ml of oxygen, over 98% of it bound. The binding curve is S-shaped: haemoglobin loads fully in the lungs yet releases oxygen readily where partial pressure is low. Acid, heat and carbon dioxide, all produced by working tissue, shift the curve to release more (the Bohr effect).

Pulse oximeters estimate the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen; 95 to 100% is normal at sea level. Anaemia lowers the amount of haemoglobin, so total oxygen delivery falls even when saturation reads normal, which is why a saturation reading alone can mislead.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 240 times more tightly than oxygen, and standard oximeters cannot tell the difference.

keyFacts.label: Oxygen per litre of arterial blood

co2-removal.name: Carbon dioxide removal and acid-base balance
co2-removal.summary: Carbon dioxide, the waste of metabolism, is carried mostly as bicarbonate and breathed out; the balance between the two sets blood acidity.
body: Tissues make about 200 ml of carbon dioxide a minute at rest. In the blood most of it reacts with water inside red cells to form bicarbonate and hydrogen ions; some binds to haemoglobin and a little dissolves. In the lungs the reaction reverses and the gas is exhaled.

Because carbon dioxide is an acid in solution, breathing controls blood pH within minutes: breathing faster lowers carbon dioxide and raises pH (respiratory alkalosis, as in panic-driven hyperventilation), breathing less does the opposite. The kidneys adjust bicarbonate over hours to days, giving a second, slower control.

Normal arterial pH is tightly held at 7.35 to 7.45. Diseases that trap air (COPD), drugs that suppress breathing (opioids) or metabolic crises (diabetic ketoacidosis) disturb this balance and are diagnosed with an arterial blood gas.

lung-volumes.name: Lung volumes and capacities
lung-volumes.summary: The amounts of air the lungs move and hold, measured by spirometry and used to separate obstructive from restrictive disease.
body: A quiet breath moves about half a litre (tidal volume). Above it lies the inspiratory reserve and below it the expiratory reserve; together with tidal volume these make the vital capacity, roughly 4 to 5 litres in an adult man. Even after the deepest expiration about 1.2 litres remains as residual volume, keeping the alveoli open.

Spirometry records the forced vital capacity (FVC) and the volume blown out in the first second (FEV1). Obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) narrows the airways so FEV1 falls out of proportion to FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio drops below about 0.7. Restrictive disease (fibrosis, chest wall problems) shrinks all volumes but keeps the ratio normal.
Volumes fall with age, height and smoking and rise with training; reference values are matched to age, sex, height and ethnicity.

neurons.name: Neurons
neurons.summary: The nerve cell: a body with branching dendrites that receive signals and a single axon that carries them onward, sometimes for a metre.
body: The brain holds about 86 billion neurons, each connected to thousands of others through synapses. Dendrites collect incoming signals; if their sum crosses a threshold at the axon hillock, the neuron fires an all-or-nothing action potential down its axon. Axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulation that lets the impulse jump between gaps and travel up to 120 metres per second.

Neurons communicate chemically: an arriving impulse releases a neurotransmitter such as glutamate, GABA, dopamine or acetylcholine into the synaptic gap, and the receiving cell is excited or inhibited depending on its receptors. Most drugs acting on the nervous system change this step.
Glial cells outnumber neurons and feed, insulate and protect them. Unlike most cells, adult neurons rarely divide, which is why injury to the brain and spinal cord is so hard to repair.

nerve-signals.name: Nerve signals
nerve-signals.summary: Information travels as brief electrical pulses, action potentials, whose rate carries the message; at synapses it becomes chemical.
body: An action potential is a wave of sodium ions rushing into the axon followed by potassium flowing out, restoring the resting state within a millisecond. Because each pulse is identical, a stronger stimulus is signalled by more pulses per second, not bigger ones.

Sensory signals travel from receptors through the spinal cord and thalamus to the cortex; motor commands travel down the corticospinal tract, cross to the opposite side in the medulla, and leave through spinal nerves. This crossing is why a stroke in the left hemisphere weakens the right side of the body.

Local anaesthetics block sodium channels so pain signals never start; multiple sclerosis strips myelin so signals slow or fail; nerve compression, as in carpal tunnel syndrome, produces tingling and numbness along the nerve's territory.

reflexes.name: Reflexes
reflexes.summary: Fast, automatic responses wired through the spinal cord or brainstem that protect the body before the brain has time to decide.
body: The knee-jerk is the simplest: tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, a sensory neuron fires straight onto a motor neuron in the spinal cord, and the muscle contracts. Withdrawal from a hot object uses one more neuron and also inhibits the opposing muscles. Brainstem reflexes include the pupil's response to light, the gag and cough reflexes and the baroreceptor reflex that steadies blood pressure.

Clinicians grade tendon reflexes because they map the nervous system: a lost ankle reflex points to the S1 nerve root, brisk reflexes with a spreading pattern point to damage above the spinal cord, as after a stroke.
Reflexes can be modulated: the brain can suppress a withdrawal to keep hold of a hot cup, and spinal cord injury releases reflexes from that control, producing spasticity.

brain-functions.name: Brain functions
brain-functions.summary: Different regions specialise: the cortex for perception, movement, language and thought; deep nuclei for movement and emotion; the brainstem for life support; the cerebellum for coordination.
body: The frontal lobe plans, decides and, through the precentral gyrus, commands movement; Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus produces speech. The parietal lobe handles touch and space, the temporal lobe hearing, memory and language comprehension (Wernicke's area), and the occipital lobe vision. The insula senses the body's internal state.

Beneath the cortex, the basal ganglia select and smooth movements, the thalamus relays almost every signal to the cortex, the hypothalamus runs hormones, temperature, hunger and sleep, and the hippocampus lays down new memories. The brainstem keeps breathing and the heart going and houses the cranial nerve nuclei; the cerebellum times and coordinates movement.

Because functions are localised, the pattern of a deficit locates a lesion: right-sided weakness with lost speech points to the left middle cerebral artery territory, unsteadiness to the cerebellum, and memory loss with preserved alertness to the medial temporal lobes.

sensory-systems.name: Sensory systems
sensory-systems.summary: Receptors convert light, sound, chemicals, pressure and temperature into nerve signals that the thalamus and cortex turn into perception.
body: The eye focuses light onto the retina, where rods handle dim light and cones colour; signals cross partly at the optic chiasm so each visual cortex sees the opposite half of the world. The ear turns vibration into fluid waves in the cochlea, where hair cells fire in proportion to pitch; the neighbouring semicircular canals and otolith organs sense rotation and gravity for balance.

Smell receptors in the roof of the nose project directly to the olfactory cortex and limbic system, which is why odours evoke memory so strongly; taste buds detect sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami. Skin carries receptors for touch, vibration, temperature and pain, with the fingertips and lips most densely supplied and therefore over-represented in the sensory cortex.
Pain is a protective signal, not a measurement of damage: it is amplified by inflammation and modulated by the brain, which explains phantom limb pain and the relief of distraction.

digestion.name: Digestion
digestion.summary: Food is broken down mechanically by chewing and churning and chemically by enzymes, from starch in the mouth to proteins and fats in the small intestine.
body: Chewing mixes food with saliva, whose amylase starts on starch. The stomach adds hydrochloric acid, which unfolds proteins and kills microbes, and pepsin, which begins their breakdown; it churns the mix into a paste called chyme and releases it into the duodenum a few millilitres at a time.

In the duodenum, bile from the liver emulsifies fat into droplets and pancreatic juice supplies the main enzymes: lipase for fat, amylase for starch and proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin) for protein. Enzymes on the intestinal lining finish the job, splitting sugars and peptides into single molecules ready for absorption.

Digestion is regulated by nerves and hormones: the sight and smell of food prime the stomach (vagus nerve), gastrin drives acid, and cholecystokinin from the duodenum squeezes the gallbladder and slows the stomach when fat arrives.

absorption.name: Absorption
absorption.summary: Nutrients cross the lining of the small intestine into blood and lymph; the colon reclaims water and salts.
body: The small intestine's folds, finger-like villi and microscopic microvilli multiply its surface area to around 30 square metres. Sugars and amino acids are pumped into the cells and pass into capillaries that drain to the portal vein and the liver. Fats are rebuilt inside the cells into chylomicrons and enter the lymphatic lacteals, bypassing the liver at first.

Iron and calcium are absorbed mainly in the duodenum, most other nutrients in the jejunum, and vitamin B12 and bile salts only in the terminal ileum, which is why disease or surgery there causes specific deficiencies.

About nine litres of fluid enter the gut daily (drink plus secretions); the small intestine absorbs most and the colon nearly all the rest, leaving about 100 ml in stool. Diarrhoea is a failure of this reclamation.

gut-motility.name: Gut motility
gut-motility.summary: Coordinated waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis) move contents along the tract, run by the gut's own nervous system and tuned by the vagus nerve and hormones.
body: Swallowing is voluntary at the start, then reflex: the oesophagus carries a bolus to the stomach in about ten seconds, and the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let it through and then closes to keep acid out. The stomach mixes with slow waves three times a minute; the small intestine segments to mix and propels to move; between meals a housekeeping wave sweeps residue toward the colon every 90 minutes or so.

The colon moves contents slowly, with a few strong mass movements a day, often after meals, that push stool into the rectum and trigger the urge to defecate. The internal anal sphincter relaxes automatically; the external sphincter and puborectalis are under voluntary control.
Motility disorders cause reflux, gastroparesis, constipation or irritable bowel symptoms; a mechanical block (obstruction) produces cramping pain, vomiting and absence of gas.

liver-functions.name: Liver functions
liver-functions.summary: The liver processes everything absorbed from the gut, stores and releases fuel, makes most blood proteins, detoxifies drugs and produces bile.
body: Portal blood arrives loaded with nutrients and anything else absorbed. Liver cells store glucose as glycogen and release it between meals, make new glucose from amino acids when needed, build and break down fats and cholesterol, and manufacture albumin and the clotting factors. Ammonia from protein breakdown is converted to urea for the kidneys to excrete.

Enzyme systems (the cytochrome P450 family) transform drugs, alcohol and toxins into water-soluble forms for excretion; this is why liver disease changes drug doses and why paracetamol overdose is so dangerous. Old red cells are broken down and their haem becomes bilirubin, which the liver conjugates and excretes in bile; when this fails, bilirubin accumulates and the skin turns yellow (jaundice).
Bile, about half a litre a day, is stored in the gallbladder and released to emulsify dietary fat. The liver can regenerate after losing more than half its mass.

pancreatic-functions.name: Pancreatic functions
pancreatic-functions.summary: One organ, two jobs: exocrine cells pour digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum; the islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
body: About 1.5 litres of alkaline pancreatic juice a day neutralises stomach acid and delivers lipase, amylase and the protein-digesting enzymes, which are secreted as inactive precursors and switched on only in the gut so the pancreas does not digest itself. When that safeguard fails, the result is pancreatitis.

The islets sense blood glucose directly. After a meal beta cells release insulin, which tells muscle, fat and liver to take up and store glucose; between meals alpha cells release glucagon, which makes the liver release it again. This pair holds blood glucose within a narrow band around 4 to 7 mmol/L.
Type 1 diabetes destroys the beta cells; type 2 diabetes is mainly resistance to insulin's signal with a gradual failure of the beta cells to compensate.

filtration.name: Glomerular filtration
filtration.summary: Blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the nephron, about 180 litres a day, while cells and proteins stay behind.
body: Each kidney holds about a million nephrons. In the glomerulus a tuft of leaky capillaries sits inside Bowman's capsule; the pressure difference drives an ultrafiltrate of plasma through a three-layer sieve that blocks cells and almost all protein. The glomerular filtration rate (GFR), roughly 120 ml per minute in a healthy young adult, is the standard measure of kidney function.

The kidney keeps GFR steady across a wide range of blood pressures by adjusting its afferent and efferent arterioles; drugs that act on these vessels (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors) can drop filtration in a dehydrated patient.
Because creatinine is filtered freely and barely reabsorbed, its blood level rises as GFR falls, which is how kidney disease is staged. Protein in the urine means the sieve is damaged.

reabsorption.name: Tubular reabsorption and secretion
reabsorption.summary: The tubules reclaim over 99% of the filtered water and salt and all the glucose, and add wastes and excess ions to what remains.
body: The proximal tubule recovers about two thirds of the filtered water and sodium and all the glucose and amino acids; when blood glucose is high, as in uncontrolled diabetes, the transporters are overwhelmed and glucose spills into the urine. The loop of Henle builds a salt gradient in the medulla that allows water to be drawn out later. The distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune sodium, potassium and acid under hormonal control.

Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption (and potassium loss); antidiuretic hormone opens water channels in the collecting duct to concentrate urine. Diuretic drugs block specific transporters: loop diuretics in the thick ascending limb, thiazides in the distal tubule.
Secretion works the other way: the tubules actively pump potassium, hydrogen ions, drugs and organic acids into the urine, which is how penicillin and many other drugs are cleared.

urine-formation.name: Urine formation and excretion
urine-formation.summary: Filtration, reabsorption and secretion leave one to two litres of urine a day, carried by the ureters to the bladder and released under voluntary control.
body: Urine is mostly water carrying urea, creatinine, uric acid, salts and any drug metabolites the body needs to lose. Its colour reflects concentration; its composition, read by a dipstick, reveals infection (leucocytes, nitrites), blood, protein, glucose or ketones.

Peristalsis in the ureters delivers urine to the bladder, which stretches to hold 400 to 600 ml. Stretch receptors signal fullness at around 200 ml; the micturition reflex contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter, while the external sphincter is released voluntarily. Children learn this control between two and four years; strokes, spinal injury and prostate enlargement disturb it.
Kidney stones form when salts crystallise in concentrated urine; keeping urine dilute is the simplest prevention.

fluid-balance.name: Fluid balance
fluid-balance.summary: Water in equals water out: thirst, antidiuretic hormone and the kidneys keep the body's 40 litres of fluid within a litre of its set point.
body: An adult is about 60% water: two thirds inside cells, the rest in the tissue spaces and in blood plasma. Intake of about 2.5 litres a day (drink, food and metabolism) matches loss in urine, sweat, breath and stool. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense a rise in blood concentration of only 1 to 2% and trigger both thirst and antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidneys retain water.

Volume is sensed separately by stretch receptors in the heart and pressure receptors in the arteries; a fall activates the sympathetic system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade, which retains salt and water and constricts vessels. Heart failure and cirrhosis activate these pathways inappropriately and cause swelling (oedema).
Dehydration presents with thirst, dark urine, dizziness on standing and a rising heart rate; in infants and the elderly it can progress quickly.

electrolytes.name: Electrolytes
electrolytes.summary: Sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate carry charge, set the water distribution between compartments and make nerves and muscles excitable.
body: Sodium is the main ion outside cells and, with its water, sets blood volume; the kidneys and aldosterone keep its concentration near 140 mmol/L. Potassium is concentrated inside cells; its blood level, normally 3.5 to 5, must stay in a narrow band because both high and low values disturb the heart's rhythm.

Calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D and is needed for muscle contraction, clotting and nerve signalling; low levels cause tingling and cramps, high levels stones, bone pain and confusion. Magnesium is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and follows potassium.
Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, kidney disease and hormone disorders are the usual causes of imbalance, detected on a basic metabolic panel.

hormones.name: Hormones
hormones.summary: Chemical messengers released into the blood that act on distant cells carrying the right receptor, coordinating growth, metabolism, stress and reproduction over minutes to years.
body: Hormones come in families. Peptides and proteins (insulin, growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone) act on surface receptors and work within minutes. Steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen) are made from cholesterol, pass into cells and switch genes on or off over hours. Amines include adrenaline, fast and short-lived, and thyroid hormone, slow and long-lasting.

The same hormone can do different things in different tissues: adrenaline speeds the heart, dilates airways and releases glucose all at once, which is exactly what a fight-or-flight response needs. Concentrations are tiny, measured in picomoles, so small changes matter and assays must be precise.
Because hormones reach everywhere, endocrine disease is multi-system: an overactive thyroid causes weight loss, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance and anxiety together.

hormone-regulation.name: Hormone regulation: the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
hormone-regulation.summary: The hypothalamus tells the pituitary, the pituitary tells the glands, and the glands' hormones report back: a chain of command that links the brain to the endocrine system.
body: Releasing hormones from the hypothalamus travel down a private portal system to the anterior pituitary, which secretes the tropic hormones: thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, the gonadotropins, growth hormone and prolactin. The posterior pituitary stores two hormones made in the hypothalamus itself, antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.

Each axis is a loop: for the thyroid, TRH drives TSH, TSH drives thyroxine, and thyroxine suppresses both. So a failing thyroid produces a high TSH, while a pituitary problem produces low TSH with low thyroxine; the pair of results tells you where the fault lies.
Stress, sleep, light and season act on the hypothalamus, which is why cortisol peaks in the early morning, growth hormone surges in deep sleep and the menstrual cycle can stop under severe stress.

feedback-mechanisms.name: Feedback mechanisms and homeostasis
feedback-mechanisms.summary: Negative feedback, where a rise in the output switches off its own production, holds temperature, glucose, blood pressure and hormones near their set points.
body: A thermostat is the model: a sensor measures the variable, a control centre compares it with a set point, and an effector corrects the error. Body temperature is held near 37 °C by the hypothalamus, which orders sweating and skin vasodilation when hot and shivering and vasoconstriction when cold; fever is a deliberate resetting of the set point by inflammatory signals.

Glucose is held by the insulin-glucagon pair, calcium by parathyroid hormone, blood pressure by baroreflexes and the kidneys, oxygen and carbon dioxide by the breathing centres. Diseases are often a broken loop: in type 1 diabetes the effector (insulin) is missing; in Cushing's disease the control centre ignores the feedback.
Positive feedback is rare and used for events that must run to completion: the surge of oxytocin in labour, blood clotting and the sodium rush of an action potential.

endocrine-glands.name: The major endocrine glands
endocrine-glands.summary: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreatic islets, gonads and pineal each make a signature set of hormones; several other organs, including the heart, kidneys, gut and fat, make hormones too.
body: The pituitary controls growth, thyroid and adrenal function, reproduction, milk production and water balance. The thyroid sets the metabolic rate through thyroxine; the four parathyroids behind it raise blood calcium. The adrenal cortex makes cortisol (stress and glucose), aldosterone (salt and blood pressure) and androgens; its medulla makes adrenaline. The islets of the pancreas make insulin and glucagon; the testes make testosterone and the ovaries oestrogen and progesterone; the pineal makes melatonin.

Less famous sources matter clinically: the heart releases natriuretic peptides when stretched (used to diagnose heart failure), the kidneys release erythropoietin to make red cells, the gut makes incretins that boost insulin, and fat tissue makes leptin, which signals energy stores to the brain.
In this atlas the pituitary and adrenal glands are modelled; the thyroid and parathyroids are not part of the dataset.

headache.name: Headache
headache.what: Pain felt anywhere in the head. Almost everyone has headaches; the great majority are primary headaches (tension-type or migraine) rather than a sign of disease. The brain itself has no pain receptors: headache arises from the meninges, blood vessels, muscles of the scalp and neck, sinuses and the nerves that supply them.

commonCauses.name: Tension-type headache
commonCauses.note: A tight band around the head, often with neck and scalp muscle tension, stress or poor sleep.

commonCauses.name: Migraine
commonCauses.note: Throbbing, usually one-sided, worse with movement, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound; sometimes preceded by an aura.

commonCauses.name: Medication-overuse headache
commonCauses.note: Frequent painkiller use (more than 10 to 15 days a month) can itself keep the headache going.

commonCauses.name: Dehydration, hunger, alcohol, caffeine withdrawal
commonCauses.note: Common, short-lived and reversible.

commonCauses.name: Infections
commonCauses.note: Colds, flu and sinusitis often bring a dull headache with facial pressure.

lessCommon.name: Cluster headache
lessCommon.note: Excruciating pain around one eye in bouts lasting weeks, with a watering eye and blocked nostril.

lessCommon.name: Giant cell arteritis
lessCommon.note: New headache over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw pain on chewing; can threaten sight.

lessCommon.name: Raised pressure inside the skull
lessCommon.note: From a tumour, bleed or blocked fluid drainage: worse lying down, on waking and with straining, with vomiting.

lessCommon.name: Meningitis and subarachnoid haemorrhage
lessCommon.note: Sudden severe headache with fever, stiff neck, rash or collapse.

urgent: A headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds to a minute (a thunderclap headache)
Headache with fever, stiff neck, confusion, drowsiness or a rash that does not fade under a glass
Headache after a head injury, especially with vomiting or drowsiness
Headache with new weakness, numbness, slurred speech, double vision or a seizure
A new or changing headache in someone over 50, in pregnancy, or with cancer or a weakened immune system

chest-pain.name: Chest pain
chest-pain.what: Pain or pressure anywhere between the neck and the upper abdomen. The chest holds the heart, lungs, oesophagus, great vessels, ribs and muscles, and pain from any of them can feel similar, which is why chest pain is assessed urgently until a heart or lung cause is excluded.

commonCauses.name: Musculoskeletal pain
commonCauses.note: Strained chest muscles or inflamed rib cartilage (costochondritis): sharp, localised, worse on pressing or moving.

commonCauses.name: Acid reflux and oesophageal spasm
commonCauses.note: Burning behind the breastbone after meals or lying flat, often with acid taste.

commonCauses.name: Anxiety and panic
commonCauses.note: Tightness with rapid breathing, tingling and a racing heart; a diagnosis made only after other causes are excluded.

commonCauses.name: Angina
commonCauses.note: Heavy, squeezing pressure on exertion or stress, relieved by rest, from narrowed coronary arteries.

commonCauses.name: Chest infection and pleurisy
commonCauses.note: Sharp pain on breathing in, with cough or fever.

lessCommon.name: Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
lessCommon.note: Crushing central pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back with sweating, nausea and breathlessness; may be silent in diabetes and the elderly.

lessCommon.name: Pulmonary embolism
lessCommon.note: Sudden sharp pain with breathlessness, sometimes coughing blood, often with a swollen leg.

lessCommon.name: Aortic dissection
lessCommon.note: Tearing pain radiating to the back, often with very high blood pressure.

lessCommon.name: Pneumothorax
lessCommon.note: Sudden one-sided pain and breathlessness, especially in tall young men or lung disease.

lessCommon.name: Pericarditis
lessCommon.note: Sharp pain eased by sitting forward, worse lying back.

urgent: Central chest pressure lasting more than a few minutes, or spreading to the arm, jaw or back, especially with sweating, nausea or breathlessness: call emergency services
Chest pain with sudden breathlessness, coughing blood or a swollen painful leg
Tearing pain radiating to the back
Chest pain with fainting, a very fast or irregular pulse, or blue lips

abdominal-pain.name: Abdominal pain
abdominal-pain.what: Pain between the ribs and the pelvis. Where it sits, how it started and what makes it better or worse point to the organ involved: the gut, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, kidneys, bladder and reproductive organs all lie here, and some pain is referred from the chest or spine.

commonCauses.name: Gastroenteritis
commonCauses.note: Cramping pain with vomiting and diarrhoea, usually viral, lasting a few days.

commonCauses.name: Indigestion, reflux and peptic ulcer
commonCauses.note: Burning or gnawing upper abdominal pain related to meals.

commonCauses.name: Constipation and irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.note: Bloating and cramping relieved by passing stool or wind.

commonCauses.name: Trapped wind and food intolerance
commonCauses.note: Bloating and cramps after particular foods.

commonCauses.name: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.note: Lower abdominal ache with burning on passing urine and frequency.

commonCauses.name: Period pain
commonCauses.note: Cramping low abdominal pain in the days around menstruation.

lessCommon.name: Appendicitis
lessCommon.note: Pain starting around the navel and moving to the lower right, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever.

lessCommon.name: Gallstones and cholecystitis
lessCommon.note: Severe right upper pain after fatty meals, sometimes with fever or jaundice.

lessCommon.name: Pancreatitis
lessCommon.note: Constant severe upper pain boring through to the back, with vomiting, often after alcohol or with gallstones.

lessCommon.name: Kidney stones
lessCommon.note: Agonising waves of pain from loin to groin with blood in the urine.

lessCommon.name: Bowel obstruction
lessCommon.note: Colicky pain, vomiting, swelling and no wind or stool.

lessCommon.name: Ectopic pregnancy
lessCommon.note: Low one-sided pain with a missed period; an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
lessCommon.note: Deep pain with collapse in an older person.

urgent: Sudden severe pain, or pain with a rigid, very tender abdomen
Pain with repeated vomiting, vomiting blood or black tarry stools
Pain with fever and inability to keep fluids down
Pain in pregnancy or possible pregnancy, especially one-sided with bleeding
Pain with collapse, a racing pulse or cold clammy skin

back-pain.name: Back pain
back-pain.what: Pain in the spine or the muscles beside it, most often the lower back. Nine in ten episodes are 'non-specific': a strain of the muscles, ligaments and small joints that settles within weeks. Persistent, progressive or nerve-related pain needs closer assessment.

commonCauses.name: Non-specific mechanical back pain
commonCauses.note: Muscle and ligament strain from lifting, posture or sudden movement; worse with movement, better with gentle activity.

commonCauses.name: Sciatica from a slipped (herniated) disc
commonCauses.note: Pain shooting down the buttock and leg below the knee, sometimes with numbness or weakness.

commonCauses.name: Degenerative disc and facet joint disease
commonCauses.note: Stiffness and ache that worsen with age and inactivity.

commonCauses.name: Spinal stenosis
commonCauses.note: Leg pain and heaviness on walking, relieved by sitting or leaning forward.

lessCommon.name: Vertebral fracture
lessCommon.note: Sudden pain after a fall, or in osteoporosis after minimal strain.

lessCommon.name: Infection of the spine or discs
lessCommon.note: Constant pain with fever and night sweats, often with diabetes or intravenous drug use.

lessCommon.name: Cancer spread to the spine
lessCommon.note: Unremitting night pain, weight loss, a known cancer.

lessCommon.name: Inflammatory back pain (ankylosing spondylitis)
lessCommon.note: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour in a young adult, better with exercise.

lessCommon.name: Kidney stones, pyelonephritis or aortic aneurysm
lessCommon.note: Back pain from organs rather than the spine.

urgent: Numbness around the buttocks or genitals, difficulty passing or controlling urine or stool, or weakness in both legs: possible cauda equina syndrome, an emergency
Back pain after significant trauma
Back pain with fever, unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer
Severe pain with a pulsating abdominal mass or collapse

knee-pain.name: Knee pain
knee-pain.what: Pain in or around the knee, the body's largest joint, where the femur, tibia and patella meet, cushioned by the menisci and held by four main ligaments. Causes divide into injury, wear and inflammation.

commonCauses.name: Osteoarthritis
commonCauses.note: Ache and stiffness that build over months or years, worse after activity and at the end of the day, with creaking and swelling.

commonCauses.name: Ligament injuries
commonCauses.note: A twist or blow tears the anterior cruciate (a pop, rapid swelling, giving way) or the medial collateral ligament (pain on the inner side).

commonCauses.name: Meniscal tears
commonCauses.note: Twisting injuries or wear produce pain on the joint line, catching and locking.

commonCauses.name: Patellofemoral pain and runner's knee
commonCauses.note: Pain at the front of the knee with stairs, squatting and sitting.

commonCauses.name: Tendon and bursa problems
commonCauses.note: Patellar tendinopathy in jumpers, iliotibial band syndrome in runners, bursitis from kneeling.

lessCommon.name: Gout and pseudogout
lessCommon.note: A red, hot, exquisitely tender joint appearing overnight.

lessCommon.name: Septic arthritis
lessCommon.note: Hot swollen joint with fever; an emergency that destroys cartilage within days.

lessCommon.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
lessCommon.note: Symmetrical swelling with prolonged morning stiffness.

lessCommon.name: Referred pain from the hip
lessCommon.note: Especially in children and adolescents.

lessCommon.name: Baker's cyst
lessCommon.note: A swelling behind the knee from joint fluid.

urgent: A hot, swollen knee with fever or feeling unwell
Inability to bear weight, obvious deformity or a knee that locks after injury
Sudden calf pain and swelling behind the knee (possible clot)
Numbness or a cold, pale foot after injury

shortness-of-breath.name: Shortness of breath
shortness-of-breath.what: The sensation of not getting enough air. It arises when breathing demands more effort than expected, when the blood carries too little oxygen or too much carbon dioxide, or when the heart cannot keep up. Speed of onset is the key clue: seconds, hours, days or months.

commonCauses.name: Asthma
commonCauses.note: Wheeze, cough and tightness that come and go, worse at night or with triggers.

commonCauses.name: Chest infections and pneumonia
commonCauses.note: Cough, fever and breathlessness over days.

commonCauses.name: COPD
commonCauses.note: Progressive breathlessness on exertion in smokers, with chronic cough.

commonCauses.name: Heart failure
commonCauses.note: Breathless lying flat, waking at night gasping, swollen ankles.

commonCauses.name: Anaemia and deconditioning
commonCauses.note: Gradual breathlessness on effort without chest signs.

commonCauses.name: Anxiety and hyperventilation
commonCauses.note: Air hunger with tingling fingers and light-headedness.

lessCommon.name: Pulmonary embolism
lessCommon.note: Sudden breathlessness with pleuritic pain, fast pulse, sometimes a swollen leg.

lessCommon.name: Pneumothorax
lessCommon.note: Sudden one-sided breathlessness and chest pain.

lessCommon.name: Heart attack or arrhythmia
lessCommon.note: Breathlessness can be the main symptom, especially in women, the elderly and people with diabetes.

lessCommon.name: Anaphylaxis or airway obstruction
lessCommon.note: Swelling of lips and tongue, stridor, hives.

lessCommon.name: Interstitial lung disease
lessCommon.note: Slowly progressive breathlessness with a dry cough and crackles.

urgent: Breathlessness that comes on suddenly or is severe at rest
Blue lips, confusion, or inability to speak in full sentences
Breathlessness with chest pain, coughing blood or a swollen leg
Swelling of the face or tongue, or noisy breathing (stridor)
Oxygen saturation below 92% on a home oximeter

dizziness.name: Dizziness
dizziness.what: An umbrella word for several sensations: vertigo (the room spins, an inner-ear or brain problem), light-headedness (about to faint, usually a blood-flow problem), imbalance, and vague woozy feelings. Sorting out which one the person means is the first step.

commonCauses.name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
commonCauses.note: Brief spinning triggered by rolling over or looking up, from loose crystals in the inner ear.

commonCauses.name: Vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis
commonCauses.note: Days of constant vertigo with nausea after a viral infection.

commonCauses.name: Postural (orthostatic) hypotension
commonCauses.note: Light-headedness on standing, common with dehydration, blood pressure tablets and age.

commonCauses.name: Migraine
commonCauses.note: Vertigo can occur with or without headache.

commonCauses.name: Anxiety and hyperventilation
commonCauses.note: Floating, unreal feelings with rapid breathing.

commonCauses.name: Medication side effects and alcohol
commonCauses.note: Sedatives, blood pressure drugs and anticonvulsants are frequent culprits.

lessCommon.name: Stroke or TIA in the brainstem or cerebellum
lessCommon.note: Sudden vertigo with double vision, slurred speech, weakness or inability to walk.

lessCommon.name: Heart rhythm problems
lessCommon.note: Dizziness with palpitations or blackouts.

lessCommon.name: Meniere's disease
lessCommon.note: Attacks of vertigo with hearing loss, ringing and ear fullness.

lessCommon.name: Anaemia, low blood sugar or heart valve disease
lessCommon.note: Faintness on exertion.

urgent: Dizziness with new weakness, numbness, slurred speech, double vision or difficulty walking
Dizziness with chest pain, palpitations or a blackout
Dizziness with a severe headache or after a head injury
Vertigo with sudden hearing loss

fatigue.name: Fatigue
fatigue.what: Persistent tiredness that rest does not fix. It is one of the commonest reasons to see a doctor and usually reflects sleep, mood, workload or lifestyle rather than disease, but it is also the presenting feature of anaemia, thyroid disease, diabetes, infections and heart, lung, liver and kidney conditions.

commonCauses.name: Poor or short sleep
commonCauses.note: Including shift work, insomnia and obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring, unrefreshing sleep, daytime dozing).

commonCauses.name: Depression and anxiety
commonCauses.note: Low mood, loss of interest, early waking and poor concentration.

commonCauses.name: Anaemia
commonCauses.note: Especially iron deficiency in menstruating women and people with poor diet or bleeding.

commonCauses.name: Underactive thyroid
commonCauses.note: Weight gain, feeling cold, constipation and dry skin.

commonCauses.name: Viral infections and their aftermath
commonCauses.note: Glandular fever, flu, COVID-19 and other infections can leave weeks of fatigue.

commonCauses.name: Lifestyle
commonCauses.note: Alcohol, inactivity, excess caffeine, crash dieting.

lessCommon.name: Diabetes
lessCommon.note: With thirst, frequent urination and weight loss.

lessCommon.name: Heart failure, COPD, kidney and liver disease
lessCommon.note: Fatigue with breathlessness, swelling or jaundice.

lessCommon.name: Coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease
lessCommon.note: Fatigue with bowel symptoms and weight loss.

lessCommon.name: Chronic fatigue syndrome / ME
lessCommon.note: Disabling fatigue over six months, worsened by exertion, diagnosed after excluding other causes.

lessCommon.name: Cancer
lessCommon.note: With weight loss, night sweats or a lump.

lessCommon.name: Medication side effects
lessCommon.note: Beta blockers, antihistamines, opioids, antidepressants.

urgent: Fatigue with chest pain, breathlessness at rest or fainting
Fatigue with unexplained weight loss, night sweats, persistent fever or bleeding
Thoughts of self-harm alongside exhaustion and low mood

nausea.name: Nausea
nausea.what: The unpleasant sensation of being about to vomit. It is coordinated by centres in the medulla that respond to signals from the gut, the inner ear, the blood (toxins, drugs, hormones) and the higher brain (smells, fear, pain).

commonCauses.name: Gastroenteritis and food poisoning
commonCauses.note: With vomiting, diarrhoea and cramps.

commonCauses.name: Medications
commonCauses.note: Antibiotics, painkillers (opioids, NSAIDs), chemotherapy, iron, metformin.

commonCauses.name: Early pregnancy
commonCauses.note: Morning sickness in the first trimester.

commonCauses.name: Migraine
commonCauses.note: Nausea accompanies most attacks.

commonCauses.name: Motion sickness and inner ear disorders
commonCauses.note: With vertigo.

commonCauses.name: Reflux, gastritis and overeating
commonCauses.note: Upper abdominal discomfort with nausea after meals.

lessCommon.name: Bowel obstruction or appendicitis
lessCommon.note: Nausea with pain and a swollen abdomen.

lessCommon.name: Heart attack
lessCommon.note: Nausea and sweating may be the only symptoms, especially in women and diabetics.

lessCommon.name: Raised pressure in the skull
lessCommon.note: Morning nausea and headache.

lessCommon.name: Kidney failure, liver failure, diabetic ketoacidosis
lessCommon.note: Metabolic causes with drowsiness.

lessCommon.name: Gallstones and pancreatitis
lessCommon.note: With upper abdominal pain.

urgent: Nausea with chest pain, sweating or breathlessness
Nausea with severe abdominal pain or a swollen, rigid abdomen
Nausea with a severe headache, stiff neck or confusion
Persistent nausea in pregnancy with inability to keep fluids down

vomiting.name: Vomiting
vomiting.what: Forceful emptying of the stomach through the mouth, a protective reflex run by the brainstem that closes the airway, tenses the abdominal wall and reverses the direction of gut contractions. A day or two of vomiting is usually harmless; persistent, bloody or painful vomiting is not.

commonCauses.name: Gastroenteritis
commonCauses.note: Viral (norovirus, rotavirus) or bacterial; sudden onset, often with diarrhoea.

commonCauses.name: Food poisoning
commonCauses.note: Hours after a meal, often affecting several people.

commonCauses.name: Pregnancy
commonCauses.note: Hyperemesis when severe.

commonCauses.name: Reflux and gastric outlet problems
commonCauses.note: Vomiting undigested food some time after eating.

lessCommon.name: Bowel obstruction
lessCommon.note: Green (bile-stained) or faeculent vomit with pain and distension.

lessCommon.name: Appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis
lessCommon.note: Vomiting with localised pain.

lessCommon.name: Bleeding from the stomach or oesophagus
lessCommon.note: Vomiting blood or material like coffee grounds.

lessCommon.name: Head injury, meningitis, raised intracranial pressure
lessCommon.note: Vomiting with headache, drowsiness or after trauma.

lessCommon.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
lessCommon.note: Vomiting with thirst, deep breathing and drowsiness in a diabetic.

lessCommon.name: Pyloric stenosis in infants
lessCommon.note: Projectile vomiting in the first weeks of life.

urgent: Vomiting blood or black material like coffee grounds
Green or faecal-smelling vomit with a swollen painful abdomen
Vomiting after a head injury, or with severe headache, stiff neck or confusion
Signs of dehydration: very dark urine or none for 8 hours, dizziness on standing, confusion; in babies a sunken soft spot and few wet nappies
Vomiting for more than two days, or any vomiting in a baby under three months

fever.name: Fever
fever.what: A body temperature of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or more, produced when the hypothalamus raises its set point in response to inflammatory signals, most often from infection. Fever is a response, not a disease, and it helps the immune system; the cause and the person's overall condition matter more than the number.

commonCauses.name: Viral infections
commonCauses.note: Colds, flu, COVID-19, glandular fever; usually with sore throat, cough or aches.

commonCauses.name: Bacterial infections
commonCauses.note: Tonsillitis, ear infection, chest infection, urinary infection, cellulitis, dental abscess.

commonCauses.name: Vaccination reactions
commonCauses.note: Mild, brief fever within a day or two.

commonCauses.name: Childhood viral illnesses
commonCauses.note: Roseola, hand-foot-and-mouth and many others.

lessCommon.name: Sepsis
lessCommon.note: Infection overwhelming the body: fast breathing, fast pulse, confusion, mottled skin, low urine output.

lessCommon.name: Meningitis
lessCommon.note: Fever with headache, stiff neck, light sensitivity, a non-blanching rash.

lessCommon.name: Pneumonia, pyelonephritis, endocarditis, abscesses
lessCommon.note: Deep-seated bacterial infections.

lessCommon.name: Tropical infections
lessCommon.note: Malaria, dengue and typhoid after travel.

lessCommon.name: Non-infectious causes
lessCommon.note: Inflammatory diseases, some cancers (lymphoma), drug reactions, heat stroke.

urgent: Fever with a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, a stiff neck, or severe headache
Fever with fast breathing, chest pain, confusion, drowsiness or mottled cold skin
Fever in a baby under three months (38 °C or more) or under six months (39 °C or more)
Fever with a seizure, or in someone on chemotherapy or with a weakened immune system
Fever after travel to a malaria area
A temperature above 40 °C, or fever lasting more than five days

cough.name: Cough
cough.what: A reflex blast of air that clears the airways of mucus, irritants and foreign material. An acute cough (under three weeks) almost always follows a viral infection; a chronic cough (over eight weeks) needs a cause found.

commonCauses.name: Viral upper respiratory infection
commonCauses.note: Cold or flu; cough can linger for weeks after other symptoms settle.

commonCauses.name: Acute bronchitis
commonCauses.note: Productive cough after a cold, usually viral.

commonCauses.name: Asthma
commonCauses.note: Dry cough worse at night or with exercise and cold air; may be the only symptom.

commonCauses.name: Post-nasal drip and rhinitis
commonCauses.note: Tickly cough with a blocked or runny nose and throat clearing.

commonCauses.name: Acid reflux
commonCauses.note: Cough worse lying down or after meals.

commonCauses.name: Smoking and COPD
commonCauses.note: Morning cough with phlegm.

commonCauses.name: ACE inhibitor tablets
commonCauses.note: A dry cough in up to 1 in 10 people taking them.

lessCommon.name: Pneumonia
lessCommon.note: Cough with fever, breathlessness and chest pain.

lessCommon.name: Whooping cough
lessCommon.note: Bouts of coughing ending in a gasp or vomiting.

lessCommon.name: Tuberculosis
lessCommon.note: Cough over three weeks with night sweats, weight loss, sometimes blood.

lessCommon.name: Lung cancer
lessCommon.note: New or changed cough in a smoker, with blood, weight loss or hoarseness.

lessCommon.name: Heart failure and pulmonary embolism
lessCommon.note: Cough with breathlessness, frothy sputum or blood.

lessCommon.name: Inhaled foreign body
lessCommon.note: Sudden cough and wheeze, especially in toddlers.

urgent: Coughing up blood
Cough with severe breathlessness, blue lips or chest pain
Cough lasting more than three weeks, especially with weight loss, night sweats or hoarseness
A child with noisy breathing, drawing in of the ribs or drooling and difficulty swallowing

swelling.name: Swelling (oedema)
swelling.what: Excess fluid in the tissues. Swelling of both ankles that pits when pressed usually means fluid retention from the heart, kidneys, liver or medications; swelling of one limb suggests a local problem such as a clot or infection; a swollen joint points to the joint itself.

commonCauses.name: Prolonged standing, heat and pregnancy
commonCauses.note: Mild ankle swelling that clears overnight.

commonCauses.name: Medications
commonCauses.note: Calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine), NSAIDs, steroids, some diabetes drugs.

commonCauses.name: Chronic venous insufficiency and varicose veins
commonCauses.note: Aching heavy legs with skin discolouration.

commonCauses.name: Heart failure
commonCauses.note: Ankle swelling with breathlessness, especially lying flat.

commonCauses.name: Injury, sprain or insect bite
commonCauses.note: Local swelling with pain and warmth.

lessCommon.name: Deep vein thrombosis
lessCommon.note: One calf swollen, tender and warm; a clot can travel to the lungs.

lessCommon.name: Cellulitis
lessCommon.note: Spreading red, hot, painful swelling with fever.

lessCommon.name: Kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome)
lessCommon.note: Puffy eyes in the morning, frothy urine, generalised swelling.

lessCommon.name: Liver cirrhosis
lessCommon.note: Swollen abdomen (ascites) and legs with jaundice.

lessCommon.name: Lymphoedema
lessCommon.note: Firm swelling after lymph node surgery or radiotherapy.

lessCommon.name: Angioedema and anaphylaxis
lessCommon.note: Sudden swelling of lips, tongue and face.

urgent: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue, or with difficulty breathing
A single swollen, painful, warm leg, particularly after travel, surgery or immobility
Swelling with chest pain or sudden breathlessness
Red, hot, spreading swelling with fever

rash.name: Rash
rash.what: Any change in the colour or texture of the skin. Most rashes are harmless reactions, infections or inflammatory skin conditions; a few signal serious illness, especially when they come with fever, spread quickly or do not fade under pressure.

commonCauses.name: Eczema (atopic dermatitis)
commonCauses.note: Dry, itchy patches in the creases of elbows and knees.

commonCauses.name: Contact dermatitis and irritants
commonCauses.note: Red itchy skin where something touched it: nickel, detergents, plants.

commonCauses.name: Hives (urticaria)
commonCauses.note: Itchy raised wheals that move around within hours, from allergy, infection or no clear cause.

commonCauses.name: Viral rashes
commonCauses.note: Chickenpox, measles, slapped cheek, hand-foot-and-mouth; often with fever.

commonCauses.name: Fungal infections
commonCauses.note: Ringworm, athlete's foot, thrush.

commonCauses.name: Psoriasis
commonCauses.note: Well-defined red plaques with silvery scale on elbows, knees and scalp.

lessCommon.name: Meningococcal sepsis
lessCommon.note: Purple spots or bruises that do not fade under a glass, with fever and being very unwell.

lessCommon.name: Drug reactions
lessCommon.note: Widespread rash days after starting a medicine; blistering or peeling is an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Shingles
lessCommon.note: A painful band of blisters on one side of the body.

lessCommon.name: Cellulitis
lessCommon.note: Spreading, hot, tender redness.

lessCommon.name: Autoimmune disease
lessCommon.note: Butterfly rash of lupus, the rash of dermatomyositis.

lessCommon.name: Skin cancer
lessCommon.note: A changing mole or a sore that will not heal.

urgent: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, especially with fever or drowsiness
A rash with swelling of the face or tongue, wheeze or difficulty breathing
Blistering, peeling skin, or a rash affecting the mouth, eyes or genitals after a new medicine
A rapidly spreading hot, painful rash with fever

numbness.name: Numbness
numbness.what: Reduced or absent feeling in part of the body. Its distribution maps the fault: a glove or stocking pattern points to a general nerve disorder (neuropathy), a single nerve's territory to compression, one side of the body to the brain or spinal cord.

commonCauses.name: Pressure on a nerve
commonCauses.note: Sitting on a foot, sleeping on an arm: resolves in minutes.

commonCauses.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
commonCauses.note: Numb thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night, from median nerve compression at the wrist.

commonCauses.name: Sciatica or a trapped nerve in the neck
commonCauses.note: Numbness in a strip down the leg or arm with back or neck pain.

commonCauses.name: Peripheral neuropathy
commonCauses.note: Gradual glove-and-stocking numbness from diabetes, alcohol, vitamin B12 deficiency or chemotherapy.

commonCauses.name: Migraine aura
commonCauses.note: Tingling spreading up an arm to the face over minutes, followed by headache.

commonCauses.name: Hyperventilation and anxiety
commonCauses.note: Numbness around the mouth and fingertips.

lessCommon.name: Stroke or transient ischaemic attack
lessCommon.note: Sudden numbness of the face, arm or leg on one side.

lessCommon.name: Multiple sclerosis
lessCommon.note: Episodes of numbness lasting days to weeks, often with vision or balance problems.

lessCommon.name: Spinal cord compression
lessCommon.note: Numbness below a level on the trunk with weakness and bladder problems.

lessCommon.name: Cauda equina syndrome
lessCommon.note: Numbness in the saddle area with bladder or bowel disturbance.

lessCommon.name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
lessCommon.note: Ascending numbness and weakness over days after an infection.

urgent: Sudden numbness on one side of the body, face droop or slurred speech: possible stroke, call emergency services
Numbness in the saddle area with difficulty passing urine or controlling bowels
Rapidly spreading numbness and weakness
Numbness after a neck or back injury

tingling.name: Tingling (pins and needles)
tingling.what: Prickling, buzzing or crawling sensations without an outside cause, produced when sensory nerves fire abnormally. Brief tingling from pressure is universal; persistent or spreading tingling has the same causes as numbness and is investigated the same way.

commonCauses.name: Pressure on a nerve or reduced blood flow
commonCauses.note: Crossed legs, tight straps, cold hands.

commonCauses.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar nerve entrapment
commonCauses.note: Tingling in specific fingers, worse at night or leaning on the elbow.

commonCauses.name: Cervical or lumbar nerve root irritation
commonCauses.note: Tingling down an arm or leg with neck or back pain.

commonCauses.name: Hyperventilation
commonCauses.note: Tingling around the lips and in both hands during panic or over-breathing.

commonCauses.name: Peripheral neuropathy
commonCauses.note: Diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, some medicines.

lessCommon.name: Stroke or TIA
lessCommon.note: Sudden one-sided tingling with weakness or speech difficulty.

lessCommon.name: Multiple sclerosis
lessCommon.note: Tingling that spreads over days, sometimes an electric shock down the spine on bending the neck.

lessCommon.name: Low calcium or other electrolyte disturbance
lessCommon.note: Tingling around the mouth and cramps.

lessCommon.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
lessCommon.note: Tingling feet with unsteadiness and anaemia.

lessCommon.name: Raynaud's phenomenon
lessCommon.note: Fingers turn white then blue and tingle in the cold.

urgent: Sudden tingling on one side with weakness, face droop or difficulty speaking
Tingling spreading rapidly up the legs or arms over hours to days
Tingling with severe headache, neck injury or loss of bladder control

weakness.name: Weakness
weakness.what: Loss of muscle power, distinct from tiredness or heaviness. True weakness means a muscle cannot do what it could before, and its pattern (one side, one limb, both legs, face and eyes, or everywhere) points to the brain, spinal cord, nerve, junction or muscle.

commonCauses.name: Deconditioning, illness and age
commonCauses.note: Generalised weakness after bed rest, infection or with muscle loss in older age.

commonCauses.name: Nerve compression
commonCauses.note: Foot drop from a slipped disc, wrist weakness from radial nerve pressure, hand weakness from carpal tunnel or ulnar nerve entrapment.

commonCauses.name: Bell's palsy
commonCauses.note: Sudden weakness of one side of the face including the forehead.

commonCauses.name: Low potassium, thyroid disease, steroids
commonCauses.note: Generalised or proximal weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, lifting arms).

commonCauses.name: Statin and other drug-induced myopathy
commonCauses.note: Aching weak thighs and shoulders.

lessCommon.name: Stroke and TIA
lessCommon.note: Sudden weakness of the face, arm or leg on one side.

lessCommon.name: Spinal cord compression
lessCommon.note: Weakness of both legs with numbness and bladder problems.

lessCommon.name: Guillain-Barre syndrome
lessCommon.note: Ascending weakness over days, can affect breathing.

lessCommon.name: Myasthenia gravis
lessCommon.note: Fatigable weakness: drooping eyelids, double vision, worse as the day goes on.

lessCommon.name: Motor neurone disease and muscular dystrophies
lessCommon.note: Progressive weakness with wasting or twitching.

lessCommon.name: Multiple sclerosis
lessCommon.note: Episodes of weakness, numbness or vision loss.

urgent: Sudden weakness of the face, arm or leg, especially on one side: call emergency services (stroke)
Weakness of both legs, or weakness with loss of bladder or bowel control
Weakness that spreads over hours or days, or affects swallowing or breathing
Weakness after a head, neck or back injury

joint-pain.name: Joint pain
joint-pain.what: Pain in one or more joints. One hot swollen joint, several symmetrical swollen joints, and aching joints without swelling are three different problems: infection or crystals, inflammatory arthritis, and wear or viral illness respectively.

commonCauses.name: Osteoarthritis
commonCauses.note: Wear of cartilage in knees, hips, hands and spine; pain with use, stiffness after rest.

commonCauses.name: Injury and overuse
commonCauses.note: Sprains, tendon and bursa inflammation.

commonCauses.name: Viral infections
commonCauses.note: Aching joints with flu, parvovirus, rubella, chikungunya and others.

commonCauses.name: Gout
commonCauses.note: Sudden agonising red joint, classically the big toe.

commonCauses.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
commonCauses.note: Symmetrical swelling of small joints of hands and feet with morning stiffness over an hour.

lessCommon.name: Septic arthritis
lessCommon.note: A single hot swollen joint with fever; an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis
lessCommon.note: Inflammatory arthritis linked to psoriasis, the spine or a recent infection.

lessCommon.name: Lupus and other connective tissue diseases
lessCommon.note: Joint pain with rash, mouth ulcers, fatigue.

lessCommon.name: Lyme disease
lessCommon.note: Swollen knee weeks after a tick bite.

lessCommon.name: Haemophilia and leukaemia
lessCommon.note: Joint bleeding or bone pain in children.

urgent: A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever or inability to move it
Joint pain with a rash that does not fade under pressure
Joint pain after injury with deformity or inability to bear weight

coronary-artery-disease.name: Coronary artery disease
coronary-artery-disease.definition: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty plaque (atherosclerosis), limiting blood flow to the heart muscle.
coronary-artery-disease.overview: Plaque builds up over decades in the arteries that supply the heart. When a narrowing limits flow during exertion the muscle becomes short of oxygen and signals this as angina; when a plaque ruptures and a clot blocks the artery, the result is a heart attack. It is the leading cause of death worldwide, and largely preventable.
causes: Atherosclerosis: cholesterol-rich plaque forming in the artery wall, driven by inflammation
riskFactors: Family history of early heart disease
signs: Signs of risk factors: high blood pressure, xanthelasma, nicotine staining
coronary-artery-disease.diagnosis: The story of exertional chest pressure relieved by rest is the key. An ECG may be normal at rest; a stress test, CT coronary angiography or invasive angiography shows the narrowings. Blood tests assess cholesterol, glucose and kidney function.
coronary-artery-disease.treatment: Lifestyle change and medication for everyone: stop smoking, statins to lower LDL, aspirin to prevent clots, blood pressure and diabetes control, and drugs to relieve angina (nitrates, beta blockers). Significant narrowings can be opened with angioplasty and a stent or bypassed with surgery.
coronary-artery-disease.prevention: Not smoking, regular exercise, a diet low in saturated fat and salt, healthy weight, and treating blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
coronary-artery-disease.seekCare: Call emergency services for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, or angina that is new, more frequent or occurs at rest.

myocardial-infarction.name: Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
myocardial-infarction.definition: Death of heart muscle because a coronary artery is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot forming on a ruptured plaque.
myocardial-infarction.overview: Every minute of blockage kills more muscle, so a heart attack is treated as a race to reopen the artery. Survival and the amount of muscle saved depend on how quickly the person calls for help and reaches a hospital able to perform emergency angioplasty.
causes: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with clot formation
Less often: coronary spasm, spontaneous artery dissection, severe anaemia or oxygen lack with a fixed narrowing
riskFactors: Same as coronary artery disease: smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes, family history, age
signs: Fast or slow pulse, low or high blood pressure
Crackles in the lungs if the heart is failing
complications: Rupture of the heart wall or a papillary muscle
myocardial-infarction.diagnosis: An ECG within ten minutes of arrival shows ST elevation (STEMI) when a large artery is fully blocked; troponin in the blood rises over hours and confirms muscle damage in other cases. Echocardiography shows which wall has stopped moving.
myocardial-infarction.treatment: Aspirin immediately, then emergency angioplasty with a stent to reopen the artery (or clot-dissolving drugs if angioplasty is not reachable within about two hours). Afterwards: a second antiplatelet drug, a statin, a beta blocker and an ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehabilitation and risk factor control.
myocardial-infarction.prevention: The measures that prevent coronary artery disease; after a first attack, lifelong medication and rehabilitation halve the risk of another.
myocardial-infarction.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately for crushing chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or chest discomfort with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Do not drive yourself.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.definition: A syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or can do so only at raised filling pressures.
heart-failure.overview: Heart failure is the end result of damage from heart attacks, high blood pressure, valve disease or cardiomyopathy. Blood backs up behind the failing ventricle: fluid in the lungs causes breathlessness, fluid in the tissues causes swelling. It is a chronic condition managed with drugs that reduce the heart's workload and, in some cases, devices.
causes: Coronary artery disease and previous heart attacks
heart-failure.diagnosis: Blood natriuretic peptide (BNP) is raised; echocardiography measures the ejection fraction and finds the cause. ECG, chest X-ray and blood tests for kidney function and anaemia complete the picture.
heart-failure.treatment: Diuretics relieve fluid overload; ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors prolong life in reduced ejection fraction. Salt and fluid moderation, daily weights, vaccination and exercise rehabilitation. Selected patients receive pacemakers, defibrillators or, rarely, transplantation.
heart-failure.prevention: Treating blood pressure and coronary disease early, limiting alcohol, and controlling diabetes.
heart-failure.seekCare: Seek urgent help for breathlessness at rest, waking at night gasping, pink frothy sputum, chest pain, fainting, or rapid weight gain (more than 2 kg in three days).

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.definition: A common heart rhythm disorder in which the atria quiver chaotically instead of contracting, producing an irregular and often fast pulse.
atrial-fibrillation.overview: In atrial fibrillation the sinoatrial node loses control and hundreds of electrical impulses a minute swirl through the atria; the atrioventricular node lets an irregular selection through. Blood stagnates in the fibrillating left atrium and can clot, which is why AF causes one in five strokes.
causes: Coronary artery disease and heart failure
Often no single cause in older people
signs: Pulse deficit (heart rate higher than the wrist pulse)
complications: Heart failure from a persistently fast rate
atrial-fibrillation.diagnosis: An ECG shows no P waves and an irregular rhythm. Brief episodes are caught with a Holter or patch monitor or a wearable. Echocardiography looks for valve disease and atrial size; blood tests check thyroid function.
atrial-fibrillation.treatment: Two decisions: control the rate (beta blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin) or restore rhythm (cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation), and prevent stroke with an anticoagulant when the risk score justifies it. Treat the underlying causes.
atrial-fibrillation.prevention: Control blood pressure, weight, alcohol and sleep apnoea; keep active.
atrial-fibrillation.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness, and emergency services for any stroke symptoms.

hypertension.name: High blood pressure (hypertension)
hypertension.definition: Persistently raised arterial pressure, usually defined as 140/90 mmHg or more in the clinic (135/85 on home readings).
hypertension.overview: High blood pressure rarely causes symptoms but silently damages arteries, heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over years. It affects around one adult in three and is the single biggest contributor to stroke and heart disease worldwide. Treatment is cheap and effective, yet half of those affected do not know they have it.
causes: Primary (essential) hypertension in over 90%: genes, salt, weight, alcohol, inactivity, age
Secondary causes in the rest: kidney disease, adrenal tumours, narrowed renal arteries, sleep apnoea, some drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, the pill), pregnancy
signs: Usually none; very high pressure can show retinal changes, an enlarged heart or kidney damage
hypertension.diagnosis: Repeated readings in clinic confirmed by home or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. Blood and urine tests, an ECG and eye examination look for organ damage and secondary causes.
hypertension.treatment: Lifestyle first: less salt, weight loss, exercise, less alcohol. Drugs when readings stay high or risk is raised: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, thiazide-like diuretics, added stepwise; most people need two or more.
hypertension.prevention: A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and low in salt, regular activity, healthy weight, moderate alcohol and no smoking.
hypertension.seekCare: A reading above 180/120 with headache, chest pain, breathlessness, vision change or confusion is a hypertensive emergency.

deep-vein-thrombosis.name: Deep vein thrombosis
deep-vein-thrombosis.definition: A blood clot in a deep vein, most often of the calf or thigh.
deep-vein-thrombosis.overview: Clots form when blood flow slows, the vein wall is injured or the blood clots too easily (Virchow's triad). A leg DVT causes pain and swelling; its danger is that a fragment can break off and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.
causes: Immobility: surgery, long flights, bed rest, plaster casts
Pregnancy, the combined pill and hormone replacement
Inherited clotting tendencies (factor V Leiden and others)
signs: One calf swollen more than 3 cm larger than the other, warm, tender, with dilated surface veins
complications: Post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic swelling, pain and skin ulcers
deep-vein-thrombosis.diagnosis: A clinical probability score, a D-dimer blood test to rule out low-risk cases, and compression ultrasound of the leg veins to confirm.
deep-vein-thrombosis.treatment: Anticoagulation for at least three months, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or warfarin; compression stockings for symptoms; early mobilisation. Large clots occasionally need catheter-directed clot removal.
deep-vein-thrombosis.prevention: Move early after surgery, use prescribed stockings and injections in hospital, walk and hydrate on long journeys, stop smoking.
deep-vein-thrombosis.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a swollen painful calf; emergency care if breathlessness or chest pain develops.

pulmonary-embolism.name: Pulmonary embolism
pulmonary-embolism.definition: Blockage of a pulmonary artery by a clot that has travelled from a vein, usually in the leg or pelvis.
pulmonary-embolism.overview: A pulmonary embolism cuts off blood flow to part of the lung: the affected segment is ventilated but not perfused, oxygen levels fall and the right ventricle strains against the obstruction. Small emboli cause pleuritic pain and breathlessness; a large one can cause collapse and death within minutes.
causes: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg or pelvis
Rarely fat, air or amniotic fluid emboli
signs: Signs of DVT in a leg
Low blood pressure in massive PE
pulmonary-embolism.diagnosis: Probability scoring and D-dimer, then CT pulmonary angiography to show the clot; ventilation-perfusion scanning in pregnancy or kidney disease. ECG and echocardiography assess strain on the right heart.
pulmonary-embolism.treatment: Immediate anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin, then a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin for three to six months or longer); clot-dissolving drugs or catheter removal for massive PE with shock; oxygen and support.
pulmonary-embolism.prevention: DVT prevention: early mobilisation, prophylactic injections in hospital, compression stockings, keeping moving on long journeys.
pulmonary-embolism.seekCare: Emergency services for sudden breathlessness, chest pain on breathing, coughing blood or collapse, especially with a swollen leg or recent surgery.

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.definition: Sudden loss of brain function because blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, by a blocked artery (ischaemic, 85%) or a bleed (haemorrhagic).
stroke.overview: Brain tissue dies within minutes of losing its blood supply, and the lost functions map the artery: weakness and numbness of the opposite side, loss of speech, loss of half the visual field, or unsteadiness and double vision from the brainstem. Treatment to reopen the artery works only in the first hours, so stroke is a medical emergency recognised by the FAST test.
causes: Atherosclerosis of the carotid and cerebral arteries
Emboli from the heart in atrial fibrillation
Small vessel disease from high blood pressure and diabetes
Bleeding from high blood pressure, aneurysms or vascular malformations
stroke.diagnosis: Immediate CT to distinguish a bleed from a blockage, then CT or MR angiography to find the blocked vessel. Blood glucose is checked at once to exclude hypoglycaemia. ECG, echocardiography and carotid ultrasound search for the source.
stroke.treatment: For ischaemic stroke, clot-dissolving thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel blockage within 6 to 24 hours, then antiplatelet drugs, statins, blood pressure control and anticoagulation if AF is found. Bleeds need blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulants and sometimes surgery. Rehabilitation by a stroke team drives recovery.
stroke.prevention: Treat blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, stop smoking, control diabetes and cholesterol, exercise, and manage weight and alcohol.
stroke.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately at any sign of Face drooping, Arm weakness or Speech difficulty: Time matters. Symptoms that resolve (a TIA) still need same-day assessment.

migraine.name: Migraine
