measures.meaning: ST depression, arrhythmia or a fall in blood pressure signal ischaemia.
Minutes achieved and heart rate reached; a strong predictor of prognosis in itself.
A segment that moves at rest but not under stress marks a significant narrowing.
Reduced tracer uptake under stress that recovers at rest = reversible ischaemia; fixed defect = scar.

whyOrdered: Chest pain on exertion with an intermediate probability of coronary disease
Assessing how much a known narrowing matters
After a heart attack or angioplasty, before cardiac rehabilitation
Exercise-induced palpitations or blackouts
stress-test.how: Electrodes and blood pressure cuff on; the treadmill speeds up every three minutes until target heart rate, symptoms or ECG change. Imaging versions add ultrasound or a radioactive tracer.
stress-test.preparation: Light meal only; comfortable shoes; some heart drugs (beta blockers) are paused on instruction.

interpretation.finding: Marked ST depression early in exercise
interpretation.meaning: High-risk coronary disease; proceed to angiography

interpretation.finding: Good exercise capacity with no changes
interpretation.meaning: Low risk; significant disease unlikely
Viable muscle with restricted supply, likely to benefit from revascularisation

stress-test.limitations: Exercise ECG alone misses a fifth of disease and gives false positives, especially in women and with abnormal resting ECGs; CT coronary angiography is now the first test in many guidelines.

holter-monitor.name: Ambulatory ECG monitoring
holter-monitor.what: A portable recorder worn for 24 hours to two weeks (or an implanted loop recorder for up to three years) that captures the heart's rhythm during normal life, catching the intermittent arrhythmias a ten-second ECG misses.

measures.meaning: Every beat is recorded and analysed; runs of atrial fibrillation, pauses and extra beats are counted.
The wearer presses a button or keeps a diary so symptoms can be matched to the tracing at that moment.
Slowest and fastest rates, including during sleep.

whyOrdered: Palpitations that come and go
Unexplained blackouts or falls
Looking for atrial fibrillation after a stroke
Checking a pacemaker or drug treatment is controlling a rhythm
Suspected heart block
holter-monitor.how: Three to five chest electrodes lead to a small recorder on a belt, or a single adhesive patch; normal activities continue except bathing. Implantable recorders are injected under the skin of the chest.

interpretation.meaning: Diagnosis made; consider anticoagulation and rate or rhythm control

interpretation.finding: Pause of more than 3 seconds with dizziness
interpretation.meaning: Symptomatic bradycardia; likely pacemaker
Palpitations are not due to an arrhythmia; reassuring

holter-monitor.limitations: Only useful if symptoms occur during the recording; rare events need longer monitoring or an implanted device.

spirometry.name: Spirometry
spirometry.what: A forced breath out into a tube measures how much air the lungs can move and how fast. It is the test that diagnoses and grades asthma and COPD by separating airways that are narrowed (obstruction) from lungs that are stiff or small (restriction).

measures.meaning: The volume blown out in the first second; reduced when airways are narrowed.
Forced vital capacity, the total volume blown out; reduced when lungs are small or stiff.
Below 0.7 defines airflow obstruction (asthma, COPD).
FEV1 improving by 12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator suggests asthma rather than COPD.
The fastest flow, measured at home on a hand-held meter to track asthma control.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness, wheeze or chronic cough
Smokers over 35 with symptoms (COPD screening)
Asthma diagnosis and monitoring
Before lung or major surgery
Occupational lung disease surveillance
spirometry.how: Take the deepest breath possible and blast it out as hard and long as possible through a mouthpiece, repeated three times; 15-30 minutes with a bronchodilator test.
spirometry.preparation: Avoid inhalers, big meals, alcohol and vigorous exercise before the test as instructed.

interpretation.meaning: COPD; severity graded by FEV1 as % predicted
Asthma
Restrictive pattern: fibrosis, chest wall or muscle disease, obesity; full lung function tests next

spirometry.limitations: Depends on effort and technique; normal spirometry between attacks does not exclude asthma. Not safe soon after a heart attack, eye surgery or pneumothorax.

pulmonary-function-tests.name: Full pulmonary function tests
pulmonary-function-tests.what: Spirometry plus measurements it cannot make: the total volume of the lungs including the air that cannot be blown out, and how easily gas crosses from the air sacs into blood (gas transfer, DLCO). Together they classify almost any lung disease.

measures.item: Total lung capacity and residual volume
measures.meaning: Measured in a sealed booth (plethysmography) or by gas dilution; high in emphysema (air trapping), low in fibrosis.
How much of a trace of carbon monoxide crosses into blood in one breath; reduced in emphysema, fibrosis and pulmonary vascular disease, raised in lung bleeding.
The shape reveals upper airway obstruction and the site of narrowing.
For suspected neuromuscular weakness.

whyOrdered: Unexplained breathlessness with normal spirometry
Interstitial lung disease and sarcoidosis
Assessing fitness for lung resection or chemotherapy (bleomycin)
Neuromuscular disease affecting breathing
Grading emphysema
pulmonary-function-tests.how: Sitting in a clear booth breathing through a mouthpiece with a nose clip through a series of manoeuvres, about an hour.
pulmonary-function-tests.preparation: As for spirometry; avoid smoking for 24 hours because carbon monoxide affects gas transfer.

interpretation.finding: Obstruction with high residual volume and low DLCO
interpretation.meaning: Emphysema
Pulmonary fibrosis or other interstitial disease
Chest wall, obesity or muscle weakness rather than lung parenchyma
Pulmonary vascular disease, early fibrosis, anaemia

pulmonary-function-tests.limitations: Anaemia lowers DLCO; results are compared with predicted values that depend on age, sex, height and ethnicity.

pulse-oximetry.name: Pulse oximetry and blood gases
pulse-oximetry.what: A clip on the fingertip shines red and infrared light through the tissue and reads the colour of pulsing blood to estimate how saturated haemoglobin is with oxygen. When more precision or a carbon dioxide level is needed, an arterial blood gas takes blood directly from an artery.

measures.meaning: 95-100% normal in healthy adults; 88-92% is the target in people with COPD who retain carbon dioxide.
The pressure of dissolved oxygen; below 8 kPa on air defines respiratory failure.
High when ventilation is inadequate (type 2 respiratory failure); low with hyperventilation.
Acid-base status: respiratory or metabolic acidosis and alkalosis.
Rises when tissues are starved of oxygen; a key sepsis marker.

whyOrdered: Any breathless or unwell patient (oximetry is a vital sign)
Pneumonia, COVID-19, asthma attacks, COPD flares
Monitoring oxygen therapy and ventilation
Suspected sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, poisoning (blood gas)
Sleep apnoea screening overnight
pulse-oximetry.how: The probe reads within seconds; a blood gas needs a needle in the radial artery at the wrist, which stings briefly, with pressure afterwards.
pulse-oximetry.preparation: Warm hands and remove nail varnish for oximetry.

interpretation.meaning: Hypoxaemia; oxygen and urgent assessment
Acute type 2 respiratory failure; may need ventilatory support

interpretation.finding: Low pH, low bicarbonate, high lactate
interpretation.meaning: Metabolic acidosis from sepsis or poor perfusion

pulse-oximetry.limitations: Oximetry misreads with cold hands, poor circulation, nail varnish, movement, carbon monoxide poisoning and, to a degree, darker skin; it says nothing about carbon dioxide. A normal saturation does not mean breathing is adequate.

endoscopy.name: Endoscopy (as a test)
endoscopy.what: A flexible or rigid tube with a camera passed into a body cavity through a natural opening or a small cut, so the lining can be seen directly and sampled. Each region has its own scope: the gullet and stomach (gastroscopy), the large bowel (colonoscopy), the airways (bronchoscopy), the bladder (cystoscopy) and joints (arthroscopy).

measures.meaning: Inflammation, ulcers, bleeding, polyps and tumours are seen and photographed.
Tiny samples taken painlessly from the lining for microscopy.
Polyps removed, bleeding stopped, narrowings stretched, stones retrieved at the same sitting.

whyOrdered: Difficulty swallowing, persistent indigestion, vomiting blood, weight loss (gastroscopy)
Bleeding from the bowel, change in bowel habit, positive stool screening test, anaemia (colonoscopy)
Coughing blood, a shadow on a chest scan (bronchoscopy)
Blood in the urine (cystoscopy)
Surveillance of Barrett oesophagus, ulcerative colitis, polyps
endoscopy.how: Usually a day case with throat spray or sedation; 10-45 minutes depending on the scope. Full details are on each procedure page.
endoscopy.preparation: Fasting for upper scopes; bowel preparation laxatives for colonoscopy; stop blood thinners as instructed.

interpretation.meaning: High re-bleeding risk; treated endoscopically
Surveillance interval set by number and size
Staging scans and multidisciplinary team planning

endoscopy.limitations: Invasive with small risks of bleeding and perforation; the small bowel is mostly out of reach (capsule endoscopy covers it).

biopsy.name: Biopsy
biopsy.what: Removal of a small piece of tissue or a few cells so a pathologist can examine them under the microscope. It is the only way to prove most cancers and many inflammatory diseases, and it grades and types a tumour so that treatment can be planned.

measures.meaning: The architecture of the tissue: normal, inflamed, precancerous or malignant, and which type.
How abnormal the cells look, which predicts how aggressively a cancer behaves.
Protein and gene tests on the sample (HER2, EGFR, PD-L1) that decide targeted treatment.
For excision biopsies, whether abnormal tissue reaches the edge.

whyOrdered: A lump, mass or shadow on imaging
Abnormal cells on a screening test
Unexplained organ inflammation (liver, kidney, muscle, skin)
Staging lymph nodes
Monitoring transplant rejection
biopsy.how: Depends on the site: a needle through the skin guided by ultrasound or CT, forceps through an endoscope, a punch or shave of the skin, or surgical removal. Local anaesthetic for most; results in days to two weeks.
biopsy.preparation: Blood thinners may be paused; clotting checked for liver and kidney biopsies.

interpretation.meaning: No cancer; may still explain symptoms (inflammation, infection)
Precancerous change; treat or survey
Cancer confirmed; staged with imaging and discussed by a multidisciplinary team
Too little tissue; repeat

biopsy.limitations: Samples a tiny fraction of an organ and can miss a lesion; small bleeding and infection risks, higher for deep organs.

genetic-testing.name: Genetic testing
genetic-testing.what: Reading part or all of a person's DNA (from blood or saliva) or a tumour's DNA (from a biopsy) to find variants that cause disease, raise risk, or predict which drug will work. Modern sequencing panels test hundreds of genes at once.

measures.meaning: Confirms a suspected inherited condition (cystic fibrosis, Huntington disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia).
Finds high-risk variants before disease appears (BRCA1/2 for breast and ovarian cancer, Lynch syndrome for bowel cancer).
Mutations in the cancer itself (EGFR, ALK, KRAS in lung cancer) that match targeted drugs.
Variants that change how drugs are handled (DPYD before fluorouracil, HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir).

whyOrdered: A family history of cancer at young ages or in several relatives
A child with developmental problems or an unexplained syndrome
Choosing targeted cancer treatment
Planning a pregnancy in carriers of recessive conditions
Sudden cardiac death in a young relative
genetic-testing.how: A blood or saliva sample after genetic counselling; results take weeks. Tumour testing uses the existing biopsy.
genetic-testing.preparation: Counselling before predictive tests, because results affect relatives and insurance in some countries.

interpretation.meaning: Diagnosis confirmed or high risk established; cascade testing offered to relatives
Cannot be interpreted yet; not used for clinical decisions
Lowers but does not abolish risk; the test only reads the genes on the panel

genetic-testing.limitations: Most common diseases are polygenic and environmental, so a single gene test says little; incidental findings and implications for family members need careful counselling.

microbiology-tests.name: Microbiology tests
microbiology-tests.what: Tests that find the organism causing an infection: growing it on culture, detecting its genes by PCR, its proteins by antigen tests, or the antibodies the body makes against it. Culture also reports which antibiotics work.

measures.meaning: Two bottles from separate sites before antibiotics; growth within 48 hours confirms bloodstream infection and its organism.
Throat, wound, genital and sputum samples cultured or tested by PCR.
Fast detection of viruses (COVID-19, influenza) and hard-to-grow bacteria.
Antibodies show past or current infection (hepatitis, HIV, glandular fever) and immunity after vaccination.
Bacteria, parasites and C. difficile toxin; faecal immunochemical test screens for bowel cancer.

whyOrdered: Fever with no obvious source, rigors, suspected sepsis
Pneumonia, urinary infection, wound infection, meningitis
Diarrhoea lasting more than a few days or after travel
Screening for HIV, hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections
Outbreak control and infection prevention (MRSA screening)
microbiology-tests.how: Samples taken with sterile technique, ideally before antibiotics; results from hours (PCR) to days (culture) or weeks (TB).
microbiology-tests.preparation: None for most; clean-catch technique for urine, deep cough for sputum.

interpretation.finding: Two blood cultures grow the same organism
interpretation.meaning: True bacteraemia; find the source and treat for the right duration

interpretation.finding: Skin organism in one bottle only
interpretation.meaning: Probably contamination
Antiviral treatment if early and at risk; isolation
Antibiotic changed to a sensitive agent; infection control alerted

microbiology-tests.limitations: Cultures are negative in a third of sepsis cases, especially after antibiotics; a positive result can mean colonisation rather than infection.

meta.name: Imaging
meta.about: Imaging studies: how each modality works, what it shows well and badly, radiation and preparation. Educational, not a guide to which scan an individual should have.

xray.name: X-ray
xray.how: A brief pulse of X-rays passes through the body onto a digital detector. Dense tissue such as bone absorbs most of the beam and appears white; air absorbs almost none and appears black; soft tissue and fluid are shades of grey in between. The image is a two-dimensional shadow of everything in the beam's path.
shows: Bone: fractures, dislocations, arthritis, bone tumours and infection
Chest: pneumonia, fluid, collapsed lung, heart size, tumours
Abdomen: bowel obstruction, free air from a perforation, some stones
Teeth and jaw
Foreign bodies made of metal or glass
bestFor: A first look at bones and the chest: fast, cheap and available everywhere
Following fracture healing
Bowel obstruction and perforation as a screen
notFor: Soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage, brain and spinal cord
Early stress fractures and small bone injuries (MRI or CT)
Subtle lung disease (CT)
xray.preparation: None. Remove metal from the area; tell the radiographer about any possibility of pregnancy.
xray.duration: A few minutes; the exposure lasts a fraction of a second.
xray.dose: A chest X-ray is about 0.1 mSv, comparable to a few days of natural background radiation; a lumbar spine film is around 1 mSv.
xray.risks: The radiation dose is tiny for a single film; the abdomen and pelvis are shielded or avoided in pregnancy unless essential.
xray.contrast: Barium swallows and enemas coat the gut to outline it on fluoroscopy; iodine contrast is used for joints (arthrogram) and blood vessels (angiography).

commonUses.use: Cough, breathlessness, chest pain, fever, suspected pneumonia or heart failure
Injury, joint pain, suspected fracture, osteoarthritis
Obstruction, perforation, swallowed objects
DEXA scanning uses two low-energy X-ray beams to measure bone mineral density for osteoporosis

ct.name: CT scan
ct.how: An X-ray tube spins around the body while it moves through the ring, collecting thousands of projections that a computer reconstructs into thin cross-sectional slices. The slices are stacked to view any plane or a 3D model. Iodine contrast injected into a vein lights up blood vessels and shows how organs and tumours take up blood.
shows: Brain: bleeding, stroke (once established), tumours, injury
Chest: lung nodules and cancer, blood clots in the lung arteries (CTPA), fibrosis, infection
Abdomen and pelvis: appendicitis, diverticulitis, kidney stones, tumours, abscesses, bowel obstruction
Bones: complex fractures, the spine and pelvis
Blood vessels: aneurysms, dissection, coronary artery narrowing (CT coronary angiography)
bestFor: Emergencies where speed matters: trauma, stroke, suspected bleeding, severe abdominal pain
Lung disease and cancer staging
Kidney stones (no contrast needed)
Detailed bone anatomy for surgical planning
notFor: Early stroke (may look normal for hours), spinal cord, ligaments and cartilage (MRI)
Repeated scans in children and young adults where dose accumulates
People with severe kidney disease or contrast allergy (contrast may be withheld)
ct.preparation: Fasting for a few hours before contrast; kidney function checked; a cannula placed. Oral contrast is sometimes drunk an hour before abdominal scans.
ct.duration: The scan itself takes seconds to a few minutes; the visit 20-30 minutes.
ct.dose: A head CT is about 2 mSv, a chest CT 5-7 mSv and an abdomen-pelvis CT around 10 mSv: several years of background radiation, though modern scanners use far less than older ones.
ct.risks: A small increase in lifetime cancer risk with each scan, weighed against the benefit; contrast reactions (rare) and a temporary drop in kidney function in those already at risk. Avoided in pregnancy unless essential.
ct.contrast: Iodine-based, injected into a vein for vessels, organs and tumours; causes a warm flush and a metallic taste. Metformin may be paused around the scan.

commonUses.use: Head injury, sudden severe headache, first seizure, suspected stroke or bleed
Lung cancer staging, pulmonary embolism (CTPA), fibrosis, complicated pneumonia
Severe pain, suspected appendicitis, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, cancer staging
CT coronary angiography for stable chest pain; calcium scoring

mri.name: MRI scan
mri.how: A powerful magnet aligns the hydrogen nuclei in the body's water and fat. Radio pulses knock them out of alignment and, as they relax back, they emit faint signals that differ by tissue type. Different pulse sequences (T1, T2, diffusion, fat suppression) emphasise different properties, giving unrivalled soft-tissue contrast without ionising radiation.
shows: Brain and spinal cord: stroke within minutes (diffusion), multiple sclerosis, tumours, epilepsy foci, dementia patterns
Spine: disc herniation, nerve compression, infection, cord injury
Joints: cartilage, menisci, ligaments, tendons, bone marrow oedema (early stress fractures)
Heart: muscle scar, cardiomyopathy, congenital disease
Liver, pancreas, bile ducts (MRCP), prostate, pelvis, breast
bestFor: Any question about the brain, spinal cord or nerves
Ligament, cartilage and tendon injuries of the knee, shoulder and ankle
Characterising liver, pancreatic and prostate lesions
Children and pregnancy, where radiation is avoided
notFor: Emergencies needing speed (a scan takes 20-60 minutes and the environment is hard to monitor)
Lungs and calcified structures (few hydrogen nuclei; CT is better)
People with certain implants, severe claustrophobia, or who cannot lie still
mri.preparation: A detailed safety questionnaire about implants, metal fragments, pacemakers and previous surgery; all metal removed; ear protection for the loud knocking. Fasting for some abdominal scans.
mri.duration: 20-60 minutes lying still inside a tube; each sequence lasts a few minutes.
mri.dose: No ionising radiation; the magnetic field and radio waves have no known lasting effect at diagnostic strengths.
mri.risks: Ferromagnetic objects become projectiles; older pacemakers, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips and metal in the eye can be dangerous. Gadolinium contrast is avoided in severe kidney disease and pregnancy. Claustrophobia is the commonest problem.
mri.contrast: Gadolinium, injected into a vein, highlights tumours, inflammation and blood vessels; rare allergic reactions.

commonUses.use: Stroke, tumours, multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, dementia, headache with red flags
Sciatica with weakness, suspected cauda equina, infection, myelopathy
Ligament and meniscal tears, rotator cuff tears, cartilage
Liver lesions, bile duct stones (MRCP), prostate cancer, endometriosis, rectal cancer staging

ultrasound.name: Ultrasound
ultrasound.how: A hand-held probe sends pulses of high-frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes from tissue boundaries. The depth of each echo builds a live moving image. Doppler ultrasound measures the frequency shift from moving blood to show flow direction and speed in colour. It is safe, portable and real-time, but sound cannot cross bone or air.
shows: Abdomen: gallstones, liver size and texture, kidney obstruction, aortic aneurysm, fluid
Pelvis: pregnancy, ovaries and uterus, bladder volume, prostate (transrectal)
Vessels: deep vein thrombosis, carotid narrowing, varicose veins, arterial blockages
Heart: the echocardiogram
Soft tissue: thyroid nodules, breast lumps, lymph nodes, tendons, muscle tears, abscesses
Guidance for needles: biopsies, drains, injections, cannulas
bestFor: First test for the gallbladder, kidneys, thyroid, scrotum, pregnancy and leg veins
Any test that must be repeated or done at the bedside
Guiding procedures in real time
Children and pregnancy
notFor: Anything behind bone (brain in adults, spinal cord) or air (lungs beyond the surface, gas-filled bowel)
Deep structures in larger patients (image quality falls with depth)
A comprehensive survey: it shows what the operator points at, so quality depends on skill
ultrasound.preparation: Fasting for gallbladder scans so it is full; a full bladder for pelvic scans; otherwise none.
ultrasound.dose: No ionising radiation; diagnostic ultrasound has no known harmful effects at the energies used.
ultrasound.risks: None known; brief discomfort from probe pressure on a tender area.
ultrasound.contrast: Microbubble contrast (tiny gas bubbles injected into a vein) improves characterisation of liver and kidney lesions.

commonUses.use: Gallstones, jaundice, abnormal liver tests
Kidney injury, obstruction, stones, bladder emptying
Suspected deep vein thrombosis
Thyroid nodules, lymph nodes, carotid stenosis after a stroke
Tendon tears, joint effusions, guiding steroid injections

pet.name: PET-CT scan
pet.how: A tiny amount of a radioactive tracer is injected and the scanner detects where it accumulates. The commonest tracer, FDG, is a glucose analogue, so tissues that burn a lot of sugar (most cancers, infection, inflammation, the brain and heart) light up. The PET image is fused with a CT taken at the same time to show exactly where the activity sits. Other nuclear medicine scans use tracers that go to bone, the thyroid, the heart muscle or the kidneys.
shows: Cancer: staging, finding spread, judging response to treatment, distinguishing scar from active tumour
Infection and inflammation of unknown source, vasculitis, infected grafts
Brain: dementia patterns, epilepsy foci
Heart: viable versus scarred muscle
Bone scan: metastases, stress fractures, infection, Paget disease
Thyroid uptake scan: overactive nodules versus thyroiditis
bestFor: Whole-body cancer staging in lung cancer, lymphoma, melanoma, oesophageal and head and neck cancer
Deciding whether a lung nodule is likely malignant
Fever of unknown origin
notFor: Cancers with low glucose uptake (some prostate, kidney, low-grade tumours; other tracers are used)
Small lesions under about 5 mm
Brain metastases (the brain glows with normal uptake; MRI instead)
Uncontrolled diabetes, which spoils FDG uptake
pet.preparation: Fast for 6 hours, avoid exercise for 24 hours, keep warm; blood glucose checked. Sit quietly for an hour after injection while the tracer distributes.
pet.duration: About 2-3 hours in the department; scanning 20-30 minutes.
pet.dose: Around 7 mSv from the tracer plus the CT component, in total roughly 10-25 mSv depending on protocol.
pet.risks: Radiation as above; avoid close contact with pregnant women and small children for a few hours after the tracer. No allergic risk from FDG.
pet.contrast: The radiotracer itself; the CT component may be low-dose without contrast or a full diagnostic scan with iodine.

commonUses.use: Staging and restaging cancer, planning radiotherapy
Characterising a lung nodule; mediastinal lymph nodes
Frontotemporal versus Alzheimer dementia; amyloid PET
Bone scan for metastases or occult fracture

mammography.name: Mammography
mammography.how: A low-dose X-ray of each breast, compressed between two plates for a few seconds to spread the tissue thin and hold it still. Two views are taken of each side. Digital tomosynthesis takes a sweep of images to reconstruct thin slices, reducing overlap. Cancers show as masses, distortions or clusters of tiny calcifications, often years before they can be felt.
shows: Breast cancer, including ductal carcinoma in situ (calcifications)
Benign lumps: cysts, fibroadenomas (with ultrasound to tell them apart)
Breast density, which affects both risk and how easily cancers are seen
bestFor: Population screening of women aged roughly 50-70, every 2-3 years depending on country
Investigating a new lump, nipple change or skin change in women over 40
Follow-up after breast cancer treatment
notFor: Younger women with dense breasts, where ultrasound and MRI see more
Assessing implants (MRI)
Ruling out cancer completely: about 1 in 8 cancers is missed, so a new lump is always investigated even after a normal screen
mammography.preparation: No deodorant or talc on the day (they mimic calcifications); book after a period if breasts are tender.
mammography.duration: About 10-15 minutes, with each compression lasting a few seconds.
mammography.dose: About 0.4 mSv for two views of both breasts, similar to seven weeks of natural background radiation.
mammography.risks: Discomfort from compression; a small radiation dose; false alarms leading to recalls and biopsies; overdiagnosis of cancers that would never have caused harm.
mammography.contrast: Contrast-enhanced mammography with iodine is an emerging alternative to breast MRI.

commonUses.use: Asymptomatic women in the screening age range
Lump, discharge, dimpling, in a one-stop clinic with examination, ultrasound and needle biopsy
Earlier and yearly screening for BRCA carriers, usually with MRI

fluoroscopy.name: Fluoroscopy and angiography
fluoroscopy.how: A continuous or pulsed X-ray beam produces a moving image on a screen, so the radiologist can watch swallowing, bowel movement, joint motion or the passage of contrast through blood vessels in real time. Angiography injects iodine contrast through a fine catheter threaded into an artery, mapping the vessel tree and allowing treatment (angioplasty, stents, coiling, clot removal) in the same session.
shows: Swallowing problems and reflux (barium or water-soluble swallow)
Bowel narrowing, fistulas, leaks after surgery
Blood vessel narrowing, blockage, aneurysms and bleeding points
Coronary arteries during cardiac catheterisation
Guiding the placement of tubes, lines, stents and orthopaedic hardware
bestFor: Anything that must be watched moving
Combining diagnosis and treatment in one sitting (interventional radiology and cardiology)
Checking that a catheter, wire or stent is in the right place
notFor: Routine diagnosis where a still image will do (X-ray, CT) because screening time adds dose
People who cannot cooperate with swallowing or positioning instructions
fluoroscopy.preparation: Fasting for gut studies and angiography; kidney function and clotting checked; blood thinners managed; a cannula for sedation.
fluoroscopy.duration: From 10 minutes for a swallow to 1-3 hours for complex interventional procedures.
fluoroscopy.dose: Highly variable: a barium swallow around 1.5 mSv, a diagnostic coronary angiogram about 7 mSv, long interventions much more. Skin can be injured after very prolonged screening.
fluoroscopy.risks: Radiation dose that rises with screening time; contrast reactions and kidney strain; for angiography, bleeding or damage at the artery puncture site, and rarely stroke or vessel injury.
fluoroscopy.contrast: Barium for the gut (or a water-soluble alternative if a leak is suspected); iodine for vessels, joints and the urinary tract.

commonUses.use: Coronary angiography for heart attack and angina, with angioplasty and stenting
Cerebral angiography for aneurysms; mechanical thrombectomy in stroke
Barium swallow for dysphagia; contrast studies after bowel surgery
Peripheral angiography and angioplasty for blocked leg arteries

meta.name: Procedures
meta.about: Common procedures and operations: why they are done, what happens, recovery and risks, linked to the anatomy involved. Educational; individual advice comes from the treating team.

categories.name: Operations
categories.summary: Procedures done under anaesthetic in an operating theatre.

categories.name: Heart procedures
categories.summary: Catheter and surgical treatments for the heart and coronary arteries.

categories.name: Endoscopic procedures
categories.summary: Looking and treating inside the body through a scope.

categories.name: Bedside procedures
categories.summary: Procedures done in clinic or on the ward with local anaesthetic or none.

appendectomy.name: Appendicectomy
appendectomy.what: Removal of the inflamed appendix, the blind-ended tube hanging off the caecum at the start of the large intestine. Usually done through three small keyhole incisions with a camera (laparoscopically), occasionally through a single cut in the right lower abdomen.
why: Acute appendicitis, to prevent perforation and peritonitis
An appendix mass or abscess after initial antibiotics and drainage
Occasionally, an appendix tumour found on imaging or during other surgery
before: Blood tests, pregnancy test in women, sometimes ultrasound or CT
Nil by mouth; intravenous fluids and antibiotics
Consent and marking; general anaesthetic
steps: Carbon dioxide inflates the abdomen through a port at the navel to create working space
A camera and two instruments are introduced through 5-12 mm ports
The appendix is lifted, its blood supply in the mesoappendix sealed, and its base tied or stapled at the caecum
The appendix is removed in a bag; any pus is washed out
Ports are removed and the small wounds closed with dissolvable stitches
after: Home the same or next day for uncomplicated cases
Simple painkillers; walk early
Antibiotics continued for a few days if the appendix had perforated
appendectomy.recovery: Back to desk work in about a week and to sport in two to four weeks after keyhole surgery; longer after open surgery or a perforated appendix.
risks: Wound infection (more after perforation)
Pelvic abscess
Bleeding, injury to bowel or bladder (rare)
Stump leak, adhesions, hernia at the port site (rare)
Anaesthetic risks
alternatives: Antibiotics alone for uncomplicated appendicitis: works in most short term, but about a third need surgery within a few years
Drainage and delayed surgery for an abscess

cholecystectomy.name: Cholecystectomy
cholecystectomy.what: Removal of the gallbladder, the small sac under the liver that stores bile. The commonest planned abdominal operation, almost always done by keyhole surgery. The liver keeps making bile, which then flows straight into the duodenum.
why: Gallstones causing repeated pain (biliary colic)
Acute cholecystitis (an inflamed, infected gallbladder)
Gallstone pancreatitis, once recovered, to prevent recurrence
Gallbladder polyps above 10 mm or a porcelain gallbladder (cancer risk)
before: Ultrasound confirming stones; liver function tests; MRCP or ERCP if stones are suspected in the bile duct
Fasting; general anaesthetic
Antibiotics at induction if inflamed
steps: Four ports: one at the navel for the camera, three under the right ribs
The gallbladder is retracted upward to expose Calot's triangle
The cystic duct and cystic artery are identified with a 'critical view of safety', clipped and divided
The gallbladder is peeled off the liver bed with diathermy and removed in a bag through the navel port
An X-ray of the bile duct (cholangiogram) may be done during the operation
after: Home the same day or next morning
Shoulder-tip pain from residual gas for a day or two
Normal diet resumed; some people notice looser stools after fatty meals
cholecystectomy.recovery: Most people return to normal activities within two weeks; heavy lifting avoided for a few weeks.
risks: Bile leak from the liver bed or cystic duct stump (1-2%)
Injury to the common bile duct (about 1 in 300), the serious complication
Bleeding, infection, retained stones in the duct
Conversion to open surgery (a few per cent, more in acute inflammation)
alternatives: Watchful waiting for stones with no symptoms
Antibiotics and a drainage tube (cholecystostomy) in patients too unwell for surgery
Bile-acid tablets for tiny stones (slow, often recur)

knee-replacement.name: Knee replacement
knee-replacement.what: The worn surfaces at the end of the femur and top of the tibia are cut away and capped with metal components, with a polyethylene insert between them as the new cartilage; the back of the kneecap is often resurfaced. A partial replacement treats one compartment only when the rest of the joint is healthy.
why: Severe osteoarthritis (or rheumatoid arthritis) with pain that limits walking, sleep and daily life despite painkillers, physiotherapy, weight loss and injections
Post-traumatic arthritis after fractures
Rarely, tumours or failed previous surgery
before: Standing X-rays; blood tests, ECG, MRSA screen, dental check
'Joint school' education, prehabilitation exercises, weight optimisation
Spinal or general anaesthetic with nerve blocks
steps: A vertical incision over the front of the knee; the kneecap is moved aside
Guided cuts remove a few millimetres from the end of the femur and top of the tibia, and worn cartilage and the cruciate ligaments as required
Trial components are fitted and the ligament balance and alignment checked through the full range of movement
The final metal components are cemented (or press-fitted) and the plastic insert locked in
The joint is washed, local anaesthetic infiltrated, and the layers closed
after: Standing and walking with a frame the same day or next
Physiotherapy from day one: bending, straightening, stairs; home in 1-3 days
Blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2-6 weeks; ice and elevation
Wound check at two weeks; six-week and one-year reviews
knee-replacement.recovery: Walking without aids by about six weeks, driving at 6-8 weeks, most of the benefit by three months and continued improvement for a year. A knee replacement usually lasts 15-25 years.
risks: Deep infection (about 1%), the most serious, sometimes needing revision
Blood clots in the leg or lung
Stiffness needing manipulation
Loosening or wear over time; a small number never feel quite right
Nerve or vessel injury, fracture around the implant (rare)
alternatives: Exercise programmes, weight loss, walking aids, bracing
Steroid or hyaluronic acid injections
Osteotomy (realigning the bone) in younger patients with one-sided wear
Arthroscopy is not helpful for degenerative knees

cataract-surgery.name: Cataract surgery
cataract-surgery.what: The cloudy natural lens of the eye is broken up with ultrasound through a 2-3 mm incision at the edge of the cornea and sucked out, and a folded plastic lens is injected into the empty lens capsule where it unfolds. Done under drops or a local anaesthetic injection in 15-30 minutes, it is the commonest operation in the world.
why: A cataract that blurs vision or causes glare enough to affect daily life, driving or work
Rarely, to see the retina for treating diabetic eye disease, or to lower eye pressure in glaucoma
before: Eye measurements (biometry) to choose the lens power, aiming for distance or near focus
Drops to dilate the pupil on the day; anaesthetic drops or a small injection
No need to fast for local anaesthetic; regular medicines continued
steps: A tiny self-sealing incision is made at the edge of the cornea
A circular opening is torn in the front of the lens capsule
An ultrasound probe emulsifies the lens nucleus, which is aspirated along with the softer cortex
The folded intraocular lens is injected into the capsule and unfolds into place
The incision seals without stitches; antibiotic is placed in the eye
after: Home within an hour with a clear shield to wear at night for a week
Antibiotic and anti-inflammatory drops for about four weeks
Vision usually clears within days; new glasses after 4-6 weeks
Avoid rubbing the eye, swimming and heavy lifting for a couple of weeks
cataract-surgery.recovery: Most people see well within a few days and resume driving within one to two weeks once the eye meets the standard. The second eye is done weeks later.
risks: Posterior capsule opacification (cloudy membrane behind the lens) in up to a fifth over years, cleared with a quick laser
Infection inside the eye (endophthalmitis, about 1 in 1000), sight-threatening
Tear of the capsule, retinal detachment, swelling of the retina, raised pressure
A refractive surprise needing glasses or a lens exchange
alternatives: Stronger glasses and better lighting while the cataract is mild
No surgery, if vision is acceptable; cataracts do not damage the eye by waiting except when very advanced

angioplasty.name: Coronary angioplasty and stenting
angioplasty.what: A narrowed or blocked coronary artery is opened from inside. A fine wire is steered across the narrowing through a catheter from the wrist or groin, a balloon is inflated to crush the plaque against the wall, and a drug-coated metal mesh stent is expanded to hold the artery open. As primary PCI it is the emergency treatment for a heart attack; electively it relieves angina.
why: ST-elevation heart attack (STEMI): open the artery within 120 minutes of diagnosis
Non-ST-elevation heart attack and unstable angina, usually within days
Stable angina not controlled by medication, or with a large area of ischaemia on testing
before: ECG, troponin, kidney function, clotting; a loading dose of aspirin and a second antiplatelet
Nil by mouth if elective; in an emergency straight to the catheter lab
Local anaesthetic to the wrist; mild sedation
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial (or femoral) artery and heparin given
Catheters are passed to the origin of each coronary artery and contrast injected to map the narrowings
A guidewire is steered across the lesion
A balloon is inflated for seconds to open the narrowing, with the ECG watched for ischaemia
A drug-eluting stent on a balloon is positioned and expanded to the artery's size; a final angiogram confirms flow
The sheath is removed and the wrist compressed with a band
after: Bed rest for a few hours (longer for femoral access); home the next day for elective cases, 2-3 days after a heart attack
Dual antiplatelet therapy for 6-12 months to stop clot forming on the stent, then aspirin for life
Statin, beta blocker and ACE inhibitor as indicated; cardiac rehabilitation
angioplasty.recovery: Back to light activity within days and work in a week or two for elective procedures; after a heart attack, structured rehabilitation over 6-12 weeks.
risks: Bruising or bleeding at the puncture site; rarely damage to the artery
Contrast kidney injury and allergy
Heart attack, stroke or death during the procedure (well under 1% electively, higher in emergencies)
Stent thrombosis (rare, but serious if antiplatelets are stopped early); restenosis within the stent over years
Emergency bypass surgery (rare)
alternatives: Medication alone for stable angina (equally good for survival in many cases)
Coronary artery bypass grafting for three-vessel or left main disease, especially with diabetes
Thrombolysis (clot-busting drugs) when PCI cannot be delivered in time

references.title: NHS: Coronary angioplasty and stent insertion

coronary-bypass.name: Coronary artery bypass grafting
coronary-bypass.what: Open-heart surgery that routes blood around blocked coronary arteries using the patient's own vessels: the internal mammary artery from inside the chest wall is joined beyond the blockage in the left anterior descending artery, and lengths of leg vein or radial artery bridge from the aorta to the other vessels. Usually done on a heart-lung machine with the heart stopped.
why: Left main stem or three-vessel coronary disease, particularly with diabetes or a weak ventricle
Angina not controlled by medication where anatomy is unsuitable for stents
Failed or complicated angioplasty
Combined with valve surgery when both are needed
before: Coronary angiography and echocardiogram; carotid ultrasound; lung function, bloods, dental review
Stop clopidogrel a few days before; continue aspirin
General anaesthetic; arterial and central venous lines; urinary catheter
steps: The sternum is split lengthways and the internal mammary artery harvested from the chest wall while the vein is taken from the leg
Heparin is given and the heart-lung machine takes over circulation; the aorta is clamped and the heart arrested with cold potassium solution
Each graft is sewn with fine sutures to the coronary artery beyond its blockage; vein grafts are then joined to the aorta
The heart is restarted, the machine weaned off, and pacing wires and chest drains placed
The sternum is closed with steel wires and the skin closed
after: Intensive care overnight on a ventilator for a few hours, then the ward; 5-8 days in hospital
Chest drains out in a day or two; pain from the sternum and leg wound
Aspirin, statin, beta blocker; cardiac rehabilitation from about six weeks
coronary-bypass.recovery: Six to twelve weeks off work, no driving for four weeks, no heavy lifting for three months while the sternum knits; full benefit at about three months. Arterial grafts last decades; vein grafts about half are narrowed by ten years.
risks: Death (around 1-2% electively, higher in emergencies and with other illness)
Stroke (1-2%), heart attack, kidney injury
Atrial fibrillation in a third (usually temporary)
Wound infection, especially of the sternum in diabetes and obesity
Bleeding needing a return to theatre; memory and concentration changes for some months
alternatives: Angioplasty and stents for suitable anatomy
Optimal medical therapy
Off-pump and minimally invasive bypass in selected cases

cardiac-catheterization.name: Cardiac catheterisation
cardiac-catheterization.what: Thin tubes are passed through an artery or vein to the heart to measure pressures and oxygen levels in its chambers, inject contrast into the coronary arteries and chambers, and, in electrophysiology studies, map the electrical circuits and burn or freeze the tissue causing an arrhythmia (ablation).
why: Mapping coronary artery narrowing in angina or after a heart attack (before angioplasty or bypass)
Assessing valve disease and heart failure by measuring pressures, including pulmonary hypertension
Diagnosing and ablating arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, SVT and atrial flutter
Closing holes in the heart, replacing valves through a catheter (TAVI), biopsy of heart muscle
before: Blood tests including kidney function and clotting; ECG; sometimes echo or CT
Fasting 4-6 hours; metformin and blood thinners managed
Local anaesthetic to the wrist or groin, light sedation; awake throughout
steps: A sheath is placed in the radial artery (coronaries), femoral artery (left heart) or femoral vein (right heart, electrophysiology)
Catheters are advanced under X-ray screening to the coronary origins or heart chambers
Contrast injections film the arteries from several angles; pressures are recorded through the catheter
In electrophysiology, several electrode catheters map the rhythm; pacing provokes the arrhythmia and the culprit tissue is ablated
Sheaths are removed and the site compressed or closed with a plug
after: Lie flat for 2-6 hours after femoral access; a wrist band for radial
Home the same day for diagnostic studies; drink fluids to clear contrast
Results explained immediately with a plan for medication, stents or surgery
cardiac-catheterization.recovery: Normal activities within a day or two; avoid heavy lifting for a week. Ablation for atrial fibrillation is followed by anticoagulation for at least two months.
risks: Bruising, bleeding or a false aneurysm at the puncture site
Contrast kidney injury or allergy
Stroke, heart attack, arrhythmia, perforation of the heart (all rare, well under 1%)
For ablation: damage to the heart's normal conduction needing a pacemaker (rare)
alternatives: CT coronary angiography for stable chest pain (no catheter, but no treatment possible)
Echocardiography and cardiac MRI for structure and function
Medication for arrhythmias instead of ablation

references.title: NHS: Cardiac catheterisation and coronary angiography

upper-endoscopy.name: Gastroscopy
upper-endoscopy.what: A thin flexible camera is passed through the mouth down the oesophagus, into the stomach and the first part of the small intestine, giving a direct view of the lining and allowing biopsies and treatment. It takes 5-15 minutes with throat spray or light sedation.
why: Difficulty or pain on swallowing, persistent indigestion, especially over 55 or with weight loss
Vomiting blood or black stools (urgent, to find and treat the bleeding point)
Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia
Diagnosing coeliac disease, H. pylori, Barrett oesophagus; surveillance of ulcers and Barrett
Treatment: stretching strictures, removing polyps, banding varices, placing feeding tubes and stents
before: Nothing to eat for 6 hours and clear fluids only until 2 hours before
Stop acid-suppressing tablets for two weeks if testing for H. pylori or ulcers is the aim
Blood thinners managed; a driver if sedated
steps: Lying on the left side with a mouthguard; throat spray numbs the gullet, or sedation is given through a cannula
The scope is swallowed over the back of the tongue and advanced under direct vision
Air inflates the stomach for a clear view; the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum are inspected in turn
Biopsies are taken painlessly with forceps through the scope; polyps removed, bleeding treated with clips, injections or heat
The scope is withdrawn; the whole procedure is recorded
after: Sore throat and bloating for a day
Eat and drink once the throat spray has worn off (about an hour)
No driving, alcohol or important decisions for 24 hours after sedation
Biopsy results in one to two weeks
upper-endoscopy.recovery: Normal activities the same day (next day after sedation).
risks: Sore throat, bloating
Bleeding after biopsy or polyp removal (small)
Perforation of the oesophagus or stomach (about 1 in 3000, higher with stretching)
Reaction to sedation, chest infection from aspiration (rare)
alternatives: Barium swallow or CT (no biopsies)
Capsule endoscopy for the small bowel
A trial of acid suppression in younger patients without alarm features

colonoscopy.name: Colonoscopy
colonoscopy.what: A flexible camera is passed through the anus around the whole large intestine to the caecum and often into the last part of the small intestine. Polyps found on the way are removed, which prevents them growing into cancer; this is why screening colonoscopy reduces bowel cancer deaths.
why: A positive stool screening test (FIT) or bleeding from the bowel
Change in bowel habit, unexplained weight loss or iron-deficiency anaemia
Diagnosing and monitoring inflammatory bowel disease
Surveillance after polyps or bowel cancer, and in high-risk families
Removing polyps, stopping bleeding, dilating strictures, decompressing a twisted bowel
before: Low-fibre diet for a few days, then strong laxative bowel preparation the day before, drinking litres of clear fluid until the output runs clear
Iron tablets stopped a week before; blood thinners and diabetes medicines adjusted
Sedation and painkiller through a cannula, or gas and air
steps: Lying on the left side; the lubricated scope is inserted and advanced with carbon dioxide inflating the bowel
The scope is steered around the sigmoid, descending, transverse and ascending colon to the caecum, changing position or with abdominal pressure to straighten loops
The lining is inspected carefully on the slow withdrawal (at least six minutes)
Polyps are snared with a wire loop and cut with diathermy, or removed cold if small; larger lesions lifted and resected in pieces
Biopsies are taken from any abnormal or inflamed areas
after: Wind and cramps for a few hours as gas passes
Eat and drink normally; a little blood after polypectomy is expected
No driving for 24 hours after sedation
Histology in one to two weeks decides surveillance intervals
risks: Bleeding after polyp removal (about 1 in 100 for large polyps, sometimes delayed by a week)
Perforation (about 1 in 1000-2000), more after resection of large polyps; may need surgery
Missed lesions (some per cent, especially with poor preparation)
Reaction to sedation; dehydration from bowel preparation in the frail
alternatives: CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy): no sedation, but no biopsies and needs colonoscopy if abnormal
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: examines only the left colon with an enema
Capsule colonoscopy in selected cases

bronchoscopy.name: Bronchoscopy
bronchoscopy.what: A thin flexible scope is passed through the nose or mouth, between the vocal cords and down the trachea into the bronchi of each lung, to inspect the airways, wash out or brush cells, and take biopsies. Endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS) adds an ultrasound probe on the scope tip so lymph nodes beside the airways can be sampled with a needle through the wall.
why: A lung mass or shadow on CT, to diagnose and stage lung cancer
Coughing up blood
Persistent infection or collapse of a lung segment; sampling in immunosuppressed patients
Removing inhaled foreign bodies and mucus plugs; placing airway stents
Diagnosing sarcoidosis, tuberculosis and interstitial lung disease (cryobiopsy)
before: CT of the chest; clotting and blood count; spirometry and oxygen level
Fasting 4-6 hours; blood thinners managed
Local anaesthetic spray to the nose and throat plus sedation; oxygen through the nose; monitoring throughout
steps: The scope passes through the nostril, over the back of the tongue, and lidocaine is sprayed onto the vocal cords before passing between them
The trachea and the bronchial tree of both lungs are inspected to segmental level
Saline washings (lavage) are instilled and suctioned for microbiology and cytology; brushings scrape cells from a lesion
Forceps biopsies are taken from visible tumours; transbronchial biopsies from lung tissue beyond view, sometimes under X-ray guidance
With EBUS, a needle passes through the airway wall into lymph nodes under ultrasound view
after: Nothing to eat or drink until the throat numbness wears off (1-2 hours)
Mild cough, sore throat, a little blood-streaked sputum for a day
A chest X-ray if transbronchial biopsies were taken, to check for a collapsed lung
No driving for 24 hours; results in a week or two
risks: Low oxygen and breathlessness during the procedure
Bleeding, usually minor
Pneumothorax (collapsed lung) after transbronchial biopsy (a few per cent)
Fever, infection, arrhythmia, laryngospasm (rare)
alternatives: CT-guided needle biopsy through the chest wall for peripheral lesions
Sputum cytology and blood tests
Surgical biopsy (mediastinoscopy, VATS)

dialysis.name: Dialysis
dialysis.what: Artificial replacement of the kidneys' filtering work when they have failed. In haemodialysis, blood is pumped from a vascular access through a filter where waste and excess water pass across a membrane into dialysis fluid, then returned, usually for four hours three times a week. In peritoneal dialysis, fluid is run into the abdomen through a permanent catheter and the peritoneum itself acts as the membrane, exchanged several times a day or overnight by a machine.
why: End-stage kidney disease (eGFR under about 10, or symptoms of uraemia, fluid overload or high potassium that medication cannot control)
Acute kidney injury with life-threatening potassium, acidosis, fluid overload or toxins
Some poisonings (lithium, methanol, aspirin overdose)
before: Months of planning in advanced kidney disease: education, choosing the type, vaccination against hepatitis B

Creating access: an arteriovenous fistula joining the radial artery and cephalic vein at the wrist (or a graft), which needs 6-12 weeks to mature; or a tunnelled catheter in the internal jugular vein for urgent starts
For peritoneal dialysis, a catheter placed into the abdomen two weeks before use
steps: Haemodialysis: two needles in the fistula (or the catheter connected); blood flows at 300-400 mL/min through the dialyser; heparin prevents clotting; the machine removes a set volume of fluid; weight, blood pressure and bloods are monitored

Peritoneal dialysis: 2 litres of warmed glucose-based fluid drains into the abdomen, dwells for hours while waste and water diffuse across the peritoneum, then drains out; repeated 4 times a day (CAPD) or by a cycler overnight (APD)
Diet restricts potassium, phosphate, salt and fluid; phosphate binders, erythropoietin and vitamin D replace kidney functions dialysis cannot
after: Tiredness and cramps after haemodialysis sessions are common
Regular monthly bloods, adequacy checks and fistula care
Assessment for a kidney transplant, which offers the best survival and quality of life
dialysis.recovery: Dialysis is ongoing rather than a one-off procedure; many people continue work and travel, with peritoneal or home haemodialysis giving more flexibility.
risks: Low blood pressure, cramps, nausea during sessions
Access problems: fistula clotting or narrowing, catheter infection and bloodstream infection
Peritonitis in peritoneal dialysis (about one episode every 2-3 years)
Long term: cardiovascular disease, bone disease, amyloid, anaemia; life expectancy is reduced compared with transplantation
alternatives: Kidney transplantation (living or deceased donor), pre-emptively where possible
Conservative kidney management: symptom control without dialysis, chosen by some frail or elderly patients

blood-transfusion.name: Blood transfusion
blood-transfusion.what: Donated blood components given into a vein: red cells for anaemia and blood loss, platelets for low counts with bleeding, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate for clotting factor deficiency. Each unit is matched to the recipient's ABO and RhD blood groups and screened for antibodies, and identity is checked at every step.
why: Major bleeding from trauma, surgery, the gut or childbirth
Symptomatic anaemia that cannot wait for iron or other treatment; haemoglobin below about 70 g/L in stable patients (80 in heart disease)
Bone marrow failure and chemotherapy
Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia (regular transfusions)
Reversing clotting problems before surgery or in massive haemorrhage
before: A group-and-save or crossmatch sample, labelled at the bedside from a wristband check
Consent, explaining benefits, risks and alternatives; baseline temperature, pulse and blood pressure
A cannula in a forearm vein
steps: Two staff check the unit against the patient's identity and the compatibility label
Red cells run over 1.5-3 hours (faster in emergencies); platelets over 30 minutes; plasma over 30-60 minutes
Observations are repeated at 15 minutes and at the end of each unit
Any fever, rash, breathlessness or pain stops the transfusion immediately for assessment
Haemoglobin is rechecked after; each unit of red cells raises it by about 10 g/L
after: Most people feel better within hours if anaemia was symptomatic
Delayed reactions (jaundice, falling haemoglobin) can occur a week or so later
Women of childbearing age receive RhD-matched and K-negative blood to protect future pregnancies
blood-transfusion.recovery: Usually a day-case or in-patient treatment with no recovery period of its own.
risks: Mild fever or hives (about 1 in 100)
Fluid overload in the elderly and heart failure (the commonest serious harm), prevented by slow rates and diuretics
Acute haemolytic reaction from a wrong-blood error (rare but can be fatal), why identity checks are strict
Transfusion-related acute lung injury, bacterial contamination of platelets, and iron overload with repeated transfusion
Infection transmission is extremely rare with modern screening (HIV about 1 in several million)
alternatives: Iron (oral or intravenous), B12, folate and erythropoietin for anaemia with time to respond
Tranexamic acid and cell salvage in surgery to reduce the need
Patient blood management: correcting anaemia before planned surgery

urinary-catheterization.name: Urinary catheterisation
urinary-catheterization.what: A soft tube passed along the urethra into the bladder to drain urine, held in place by a small balloon inflated inside the bladder. Used for hours during surgery, days on a ward, or long term when the bladder cannot empty. A suprapubic catheter enters through the lower abdominal wall instead; intermittent catheterisation passes a tube several times a day and removes it each time.
why: Acute urinary retention (usually from an enlarged prostate) or chronic retention with kidney damage
Measuring urine output hour by hour in critical illness and major surgery
Neurological bladder problems (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis), often by self-catheterisation
Bladder irrigation after prostate or bladder surgery, or with clots
Incontinence with skin breakdown when other measures fail (last resort)
before: Explanation and consent; checking for latex allergy and previous difficult catheters
Sterile technique: hand hygiene, gloves, cleaning the urethral opening
Anaesthetic lubricant gel instilled into the urethra and left for a few minutes
steps: The catheter (usually 12-16 Fr) is advanced gently along the urethra; in men the penis is held upright to straighten the first bend, then lowered to pass the prostate
Urine flows once the tip is in the bladder; the catheter is advanced further before the balloon is inflated with 10 mL of sterile water
It is drawn back until the balloon rests at the bladder neck and connected to a drainage bag or valve
The volume drained is recorded; very large volumes are drained in stages if chronic retention is suspected
The catheter is secured to the thigh to prevent traction
after: Daily cleaning of the meatus, keeping the bag below bladder level and changing bags on schedule
Removal (trial without catheter) as soon as it is no longer needed, usually within days
Long-term catheters are changed every 4-12 weeks; bacteria in the urine are expected and not treated unless there are symptoms
urinary-catheterization.recovery: Slight stinging on first passing urine after removal is normal; a failed trial without catheter leads to re-catheterisation and urology review.
risks: Urinary tract infection, rising with each day in place, and catheter-related sepsis
Urethral trauma, bleeding and false passage, especially in men with strictures or enlarged prostates
Blockage by debris or clots; bypassing; bladder spasm
Long term: strictures, stones, bladder cancer risk after many years
alternatives: Bladder scan and watchful measures for mild retention
Alpha-blocker tablets before a trial without catheter in prostatic retention
Intermittent self-catheterisation or suprapubic catheter for long-term needs
Sheath (condom) drainage or pads for incontinence

joint-aspiration.name: Joint aspiration and injection
joint-aspiration.what: A needle is passed into a swollen joint to draw off fluid for analysis and to relieve pressure, often followed by an injection of corticosteroid and local anaesthetic through the same needle to settle inflammation. The knee is the commonest site; the shoulder, wrist, elbow, ankle and hip (with ultrasound guidance) are also done.
why: A hot, swollen joint where septic arthritis must be ruled out (the fluid goes for urgent microscopy and culture)
Diagnosing gout and pseudogout by finding crystals under polarised light
Relieving a tense, painful effusion after injury or in osteoarthritis
Steroid injection for osteoarthritis flares, rheumatoid arthritis, frozen shoulder, bursitis and tendon sheath inflammation
before: Explain and consent; check for anticoagulants (not a contraindication for most joints), skin infection over the site, and allergy
Position the joint: the knee slightly bent over a roll; the landmark chosen beside the patella
Skin cleaned with antiseptic; sterile gloves; local anaesthetic to the skin optional
steps: A needle (18-21 gauge) on a syringe is advanced through the skin into the joint space using landmarks or ultrasound, with a giving-way as it enters
Fluid is aspirated: its colour and clarity noted (clear yellow, cloudy, bloody, pus)
Samples are sent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and crystal examination
If indicated, the syringe is swapped and steroid (for example 40 mg methylprednisolone or triamcinolone) with lidocaine is injected
The needle is withdrawn and a dressing applied; the fluid volume is recorded
after: Rest the joint for 24-48 hours after a steroid injection; ice for discomfort
Watch for a flare of pain in the first day (crystal reaction to the steroid) and for redness, fever or increasing pain suggesting infection
Diabetics: blood glucose may rise for a few days
joint-aspiration.recovery: Relief from an aspiration is immediate; steroid benefit builds over a few days and lasts weeks to months.
risks: Introducing infection into the joint (about 1 in 10,000 with sterile technique)
Bleeding into the joint, especially on anticoagulants
Post-injection flare, skin thinning or pale patch at the site, facial flushing
Cartilage damage with repeated steroid injections (limit to 3-4 a year)
alternatives: Oral anti-inflammatories and rest
Physiotherapy and bracing
Ultrasound-guided injection for deep or difficult joints
Arthroscopy for mechanical problems

meta.name: Medications
meta.about: Medication education: what a drug is for, how it works in the body, what to watch for. This is not prescribing advice; doses, choices and monitoring are decided by a prescriber for an individual.

categories.name: Heart and circulation
categories.summary: Drugs for blood pressure, cholesterol, angina, rhythm and clots.

categories.name: Pain and inflammation
categories.summary: Analgesics from paracetamol to opioids, and anti-inflammatories.

categories.name: Breathing
categories.summary: Inhalers that open airways and calm inflammation.

aspirin.name: Aspirin
usedFor: Preventing further heart attacks and strokes in people who have had one (secondary prevention)
During a suspected heart attack (300 mg chewed) and after stents
Pain, fever and inflammation at higher doses (now largely replaced by ibuprofen and paracetamol)
Pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk pregnancy
aspirin.howItWorks: Irreversibly blocks the enzyme COX-1 in platelets so they cannot make thromboxane, the signal that makes them clump. Because platelets have no nucleus they cannot make new enzyme, so one small daily dose keeps them quiet for their whole 7-10 day life. Higher doses also block COX-2 in tissues, reducing prostaglandins that cause pain, fever and inflammation.
forms: Tablets 75 mg (dispersible or enteric coated), 300 mg
aspirin.onset: Antiplatelet effect within an hour of a chewed dose; lasts the life of the platelet.

common: Indigestion, stomach irritation
Increased bruising and bleeding time
serious: Stomach ulcers and gastrointestinal bleeding (risk rises with age, alcohol, NSAIDs and anticoagulants)
Bleeding in the brain (rare)
Reye syndrome in children with viral illness: not for under-16s except on specialist advice
Bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma

cautions: Not routinely used for primary prevention in healthy people: bleeding outweighs benefit
Active peptic ulcer, bleeding disorders, severe asthma triggered by aspirin
With anticoagulants, other NSAIDs or SSRIs, bleeding risk multiplies
Take with food; a proton pump inhibitor is often added in those at ulcer risk
aspirin.monitoring: No routine blood tests; watch for black stools, vomiting blood and unusual bruising.

ibuprofen.name: Ibuprofen
usedFor: Pain with an inflammatory component: sprains, back pain, period pain, dental pain, headache
Arthritis flares and gout attacks (short courses)
Fever
Relatives: naproxen (longer acting), diclofenac, and the COX-2-selective celecoxib and etoricoxib
ibuprofen.howItWorks: Blocks the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, cutting production of prostaglandins, the local messengers that sensitise pain nerves, widen vessels in inflamed tissue and reset the brain's thermostat in fever. The same prostaglandins protect the stomach lining and keep blood flowing through the kidneys, which explains the main harms.
forms: Tablets 200-400 mg, liquid for children, topical gel for local joint and muscle pain (fewer side effects)

common: Indigestion, nausea
Fluid retention, raised blood pressure
serious: Stomach and duodenal ulcers with bleeding or perforation, especially over 65, with steroids, aspirin or anticoagulants
Acute kidney injury, particularly when dehydrated or with ACE inhibitors and diuretics ('triple whammy')
Heart attack and stroke risk rises with high doses and prolonged use, most with diclofenac and COX-2 inhibitors
Worsening asthma in sensitive people; allergic reactions

cautions: Avoid in active ulcer disease, severe kidney disease, heart failure, third trimester of pregnancy
Use the lowest dose for the shortest time; take with food
Do not combine with other NSAIDs or aspirin; ask before use with blood thinners, lithium, methotrexate
Older adults often need a proton pump inhibitor alongside
ibuprofen.monitoring: Kidney function and blood pressure for longer-term use.

paracetamol.name: Paracetamol
usedFor: Mild to moderate pain of any cause: headache, muscle aches, back pain, osteoarthritis, after surgery
Fever
First-line pain relief in pregnancy and for children (by weight)
Combined with opioids (co-codamol) or given intravenously in hospital
paracetamol.howItWorks: Still not fully understood. It weakly inhibits cyclo-oxygenase in the brain and spinal cord rather than in inflamed tissue, and its breakdown product AM404 acts on cannabinoid and TRPV1 pathways in the central nervous system, raising the pain threshold and lowering the fever set-point. It has almost no anti-inflammatory effect and does not irritate the stomach.
forms: Tablets and capsules 500 mg, soluble tablets, liquid, suppositories, intravenous infusion
paracetamol.onset: 30-60 minutes orally; lasts 4-6 hours. Maximum 4 g in 24 hours for adults (less if under 50 kg or with liver disease).

common: Very few at normal doses; occasional rash
serious: Liver failure in overdose: even 8-10 g (16-20 tablets) can be fatal without treatment, and the danger rises with alcohol, malnutrition and enzyme-inducing drugs
Rare severe skin reactions and blood disorders

cautions: Count all sources: many cold remedies and combination painkillers contain paracetamol
Reduce dose in low body weight, chronic alcohol use and liver disease
Overdose is treated with acetylcysteine, most effective within 8 hours: any suspected overdose is an emergency even if the person feels well
paracetamol.monitoring: None routinely; liver tests after overdose.

morphine.name: Morphine and opioids
usedFor: Severe acute pain: heart attack, fractures, after major surgery, sickle cell crises
Cancer pain and pain at the end of life
Breathlessness in advanced heart and lung disease and in palliative care
Weaker relatives (codeine, tramadol) for moderate pain; long-term use for chronic non-cancer pain is now discouraged because harms outweigh benefits
morphine.howItWorks: Binds mu-opioid receptors on nerve cells in the spinal cord, brainstem and brain, the same receptors used by the body's own endorphins. This closes the gate on pain signals entering the spinal cord, dampens the emotional response to pain in the brain and, unwantedly, slows the breathing centre in the brainstem, slows the gut and triggers nausea and euphoria.
forms: Immediate-release oral liquid and tablets, 12-hourly modified-release tablets, injections into vein, muscle or under the skin, patient-controlled pumps, patches (fentanyl, buprenorphine)
morphine.onset: Intravenous within minutes; oral 30-60 minutes; modified-release over hours.

common: Constipation (almost universal, needs a laxative from the start)
Nausea, drowsiness, itching, dry mouth, small pupils
serious: Respiratory depression and death in overdose, or when combined with alcohol, benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids; reversed by naloxone
Tolerance, physical dependence and addiction with continued use
Falls and confusion in the elderly; hormone suppression and immune effects long term
Opioid-induced hyperalgesia: pain becoming worse with escalating doses

cautions: Controlled drug; start low, review early, plan the stop
Reduce doses in kidney failure (morphine metabolites accumulate), liver disease and the elderly
Never crush or chew modified-release forms
Do not drive while drowsy or after dose changes
morphine.monitoring: Sedation score and respiratory rate in hospital; regular review of benefit, dose and side effects at home.

atorvastatin.name: Atorvastatin
usedFor: Lowering LDL cholesterol to prevent heart attacks and strokes
Everyone with established cardiovascular disease (secondary prevention, usually 80 mg)
Primary prevention when 10-year cardiovascular risk is 10% or more, in diabetes, chronic kidney disease and familial hypercholesterolaemia (usually 20 mg)
atorvastatin.howItWorks: Blocks HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. The liver responds by putting more LDL receptors on its surface to pull cholesterol out of the blood, so LDL falls by 40-55%. Statins also stabilise the fatty plaques in artery walls, making them less likely to rupture and cause a clot.
forms: Tablets 10, 20, 40, 80 mg, once daily at any time (simvastatin at night)
atorvastatin.onset: Cholesterol falls within two weeks; plaque benefits build over years. Taken lifelong.

common: Muscle aches (real in a minority; most reported aches occur equally on placebo)
Headache, nausea, bowel changes
Small rise in blood glucose (slightly earlier diagnosis of diabetes in those already at risk)
serious: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown, very rare), more with high doses, interacting drugs and hypothyroidism
Liver enzyme rise (rare, usually harmless), haemorrhagic stroke risk very slightly higher in those with a previous bleed

cautions: Interactions: clarithromycin, some antifungals, ciclosporin, grapefruit juice (mainly simvastatin), gemfibrozil
Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; active liver disease
Unexplained muscle pain with dark urine needs a same-day creatine kinase test
Check thyroid function before starting if aches occur
atorvastatin.monitoring: Lipids and liver tests at baseline, 3 months and 12 months; creatine kinase only if muscle symptoms.

ramipril.name: Ramipril
usedFor: High blood pressure (first choice under 55 and in diabetes)
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (improves survival)
After a heart attack
Protecting the kidneys in diabetes and chronic kidney disease with protein in the urine
Angiotensin receptor blockers (losartan, candesartan) do the same job for people who cough on ACE inhibitors
ramipril.howItWorks: Blocks the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, the hormone that constricts arteries, drives the adrenal glands to release aldosterone (salt and water retention) and thickens heart muscle and vessel walls. Less angiotensin II means relaxed vessels, lower pressure, less strain on a failing heart and lower pressure inside the kidney's filters. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which accumulates and causes the characteristic dry cough.
forms: Capsules and tablets 1.25-10 mg once daily
ramipril.onset: Blood pressure falls within hours; full effect in a few weeks. Started low and titrated.

common: Dry tickly cough (10-15%, from bradykinin)
Dizziness with the first doses, tiredness, headache
A small rise in creatinine and potassium
serious: Angio-oedema: swelling of the lips, tongue and throat, can block the airway; stop immediately
Acute kidney injury when dehydrated, on NSAIDs, or with narrowed renal arteries
High potassium, especially with spironolactone, kidney disease or potassium supplements
Harm to the fetus: stop before or as soon as pregnancy is known

cautions: Pause on 'sick days' with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever to protect the kidneys
Avoid with NSAIDs and potassium supplements; caution with diuretics (first-dose hypotension)
Bilateral renal artery stenosis, previous angio-oedema, pregnancy: do not use
ramipril.monitoring: Kidney function and potassium before starting, 1-2 weeks after each dose change, then yearly; blood pressure.

metoprolol.name: Metoprolol and beta blockers
usedFor: Angina and after a heart attack (reduce the heart's oxygen demand and the risk of dangerous rhythms)
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (bisoprolol, carvedilol: improve survival when started low and slow)
Controlling the rate in atrial fibrillation and other fast rhythms
High blood pressure (no longer first line unless another indication)
Propranolol for migraine prevention, tremor, anxiety symptoms and thyroid storm
metoprolol.howItWorks: Occupies beta-1 receptors on heart muscle and the conducting system so adrenaline and noradrenaline cannot stimulate them. The heart beats more slowly and less forcefully, uses less oxygen, and the AV node lets fewer atrial impulses through. Non-selective agents (propranolol) also block beta-2 receptors in airways and blood vessels, which is why they can trigger asthma.
forms: Tablets (metoprolol 25-100 mg twice daily or modified release once daily; bisoprolol 1.25-10 mg once daily); intravenous for rapid rate control
metoprolol.onset: Heart rate falls within an hour; heart failure benefit builds over months.

common: Tiredness, cold hands and feet, slow pulse
Dizziness on standing, vivid dreams, sleep disturbance
Erectile dysfunction
Masking the warning signs of low blood sugar in diabetes
serious: Severe bradycardia or heart block
Worsening of heart failure if started at too high a dose
Bronchospasm in asthma (especially non-selective agents)
Rebound angina, fast rhythms or blood pressure surge if stopped abruptly

cautions: Never stop suddenly: taper over one to two weeks
Asthma (relative contraindication), severe peripheral arterial disease, uncontrolled heart failure, second- or third-degree heart block
Caution with verapamil and diltiazem (additive slowing), and in diabetes
metoprolol.monitoring: Pulse and blood pressure; ECG if the rate falls below 50 or symptoms occur.

amlodipine.name: Amlodipine
usedFor: High blood pressure (first choice over 55 and in people of Black African or Caribbean origin, or when an ACE inhibitor is not suitable)
Angina prevention
Non-dihydropyridine relatives (diltiazem, verapamil) also slow the heart and treat some fast rhythms
amlodipine.howItWorks: Blocks L-type calcium channels in the smooth muscle of artery walls. Muscle cells need calcium to contract, so with fewer channels open the arteries relax and widen, lowering resistance and blood pressure and letting more blood reach heart muscle. Amlodipine selects vessels over heart muscle, so it does not slow the heart; its long half-life gives smooth 24-hour control.
forms: Tablets 5 or 10 mg once daily
amlodipine.onset: Gradual, over days; steady state in about a week.

common: Ankle swelling (fluid leaking from widened capillaries, not heart failure; not helped by diuretics)
Flushing, headache, palpitations in the first weeks
Gum overgrowth, tiredness, dizziness
serious: Marked low blood pressure, particularly with other agents
Worsening angina rarely at the start (reflex fast heart rate)
Verapamil and diltiazem: heart block and heart failure, especially with beta blockers

cautions: Grapefruit juice increases levels of some calcium channel blockers
Severe aortic stenosis, cardiogenic shock, unstable angina
Simvastatin dose is limited with amlodipine
amlodipine.monitoring: Blood pressure; no blood tests needed for amlodipine.

furosemide.name: Furosemide
usedFor: Fluid overload in heart failure: breathlessness, swollen legs, fluid on the lungs (intravenous in emergencies)
Oedema from kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome) and liver cirrhosis (with spironolactone)
High blood pressure when kidney function is poor
Thiazide-like diuretics (indapamide, bendroflumethiazide) are the gentler relatives used for blood pressure
furosemide.howItWorks: Blocks the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the segment that reabsorbs a quarter of all filtered sodium. Salt that stays in the tubule drags water with it, so urine output can rise several-fold within an hour. Potassium, magnesium and calcium are lost too, and the kidney compensates by activating the renin-angiotensin system.
forms: Tablets 20, 40, 500 mg; oral solution; intravenous injection or infusion
furosemide.onset: Oral within an hour, lasting about 6 hours (hence the name Lasix: 'lasts six'); intravenous within minutes.

common: Passing lots of urine, urgency (take in the morning)
Dizziness on standing, dehydration, thirst, cramps
Low potassium, sodium and magnesium; raised uric acid (gout) and glucose
serious: Acute kidney injury from over-diuresis
Dangerous potassium or sodium disturbance and arrhythmia
Hearing loss (ototoxicity) with rapid high intravenous doses, especially with aminoglycosides
Collapse from low blood pressure in the frail

cautions: Daily weights in heart failure guide the dose: a gain of 2 kg in 3 days often means more diuretic
Pause on sick days with vomiting or diarrhoea
Care with lithium, digoxin, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides
Severe low potassium or sodium, anuria, dehydration: do not use until corrected
furosemide.monitoring: Kidney function and electrolytes within a week of starting or changing dose, then regularly; weight and blood pressure.

glyceryl-trinitrate.name: Glyceryl trinitrate
usedFor: Relieving an angina attack within minutes (spray or tablet under the tongue)
Preventing angina before exertion
Intravenous infusion for unstable angina, heart attack with ongoing pain and acute heart failure
Long-acting isosorbide mononitrate for regular angina prevention; GTN ointment for anal fissures
