body: Carbohydrates are broken down to glucose in the small intestine and absorbed into the portal vein to the liver; fibre is the part that reaches the colon undigested, where bacteria ferment it to short-chain fatty acids that feed the bowel lining, lower inflammation and help regulate appetite. Whole grains, beans and vegetables deliver glucose slowly; refined sugar and white flour deliver it in a surge that demands more insulin.

Protein provides amino acids for muscle, enzymes, hormones and immune cells; adults need about 0.75-1 g per kilogram a day, more when older or training. Fats build cell membranes and carry vitamins A, D, E and K: unsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts and oily fish lower LDL cholesterol, while saturated and especially industrial trans fats raise it.

Salt draws water into the blood and raises blood pressure: most adults eat 8-9 g a day against a 5-6 g limit, three-quarters of it hidden in bread, processed meat and ready meals. Micronutrients matter in specific ways: iron for haemoglobin, calcium and vitamin D for bone, folate before and during pregnancy, B12 for nerves (a risk on vegan diets and with metformin), iodine for the thyroid.

effects.effect: Fibre feeds the microbiome, prevents constipation, lowers bowel cancer risk by about 10% per 10 g a day
Unsaturated fats and fibre lower LDL; salt reduction lowers blood pressure; Mediterranean diet cuts cardiovascular events by about 30%
Slow-release carbohydrate and healthy weight prevent and can reverse type 2 diabetes
Calcium, vitamin D and protein maintain bone; vitamin D deficiency is common in northern winters
Mediterranean-style eating is linked to slower cognitive decline and lower depression risk

guidance: At least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables a day (400 g), varied in colour
Base meals on whole grains and legumes; aim for 30 g of fibre a day
Two portions of fish a week, one oily; limit red meat to about 70 g a day and avoid processed meat
Salt under 6 g (2.4 g sodium) a day; free sugars under 30 g a day (about 7 teaspoons); sugary drinks are the easiest cut
Choose unsaturated oils and spreads; keep saturated fat under 10% of energy
Vitamin D 10 micrograms daily in autumn and winter in northern latitudes; folic acid 400 micrograms when planning pregnancy

weight.name: Body weight
weight.summary: Body fat is an active endocrine organ. Excess fat, particularly around the abdominal organs, releases inflammatory signals and free fatty acids that make tissues resistant to insulin, raise blood pressure and cholesterol, load the joints and narrow the airway in sleep. Losing 5-10% of body weight measurably improves all of these.
body: Energy balance is regulated by the hypothalamus, which reads leptin from fat stores, insulin, and gut hormones such as ghrelin (hunger, from the stomach) and GLP-1 (fullness, from the small intestine). Modern food environments overwhelm these signals with energy-dense, highly palatable food and reduced movement; genetics sets how strongly each person's appetite responds. Weight is therefore not simply willpower, and biology fights weight loss by increasing hunger and lowering energy expenditure.

Where fat sits matters more than how much. Visceral fat packed around the liver, pancreas and intestines drains straight into the portal vein and drives fatty liver, insulin resistance and inflammation; fat under the skin of the hips is metabolically quieter. Waist circumference above 94 cm in men or 80 cm in women marks raised risk, and BMI thresholds are lower in South Asian and some other populations.

Weight loss of 5-10% reduces blood pressure, HbA1c and liver fat, eases knee pain and sleep apnoea, and a 15 kg loss can put type 2 diabetes into remission in about half of people within six years of diagnosis. Sustainable approaches combine reduced energy intake, protein and fibre to preserve fullness, resistance exercise to keep muscle, sleep and behavioural support; GLP-1 medicines and bariatric surgery act on the same hormone pathways for those with obesity-related disease.

effects.effect: Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome; reversed in part by weight loss
Higher blood pressure and LDL, more coronary disease and stroke
Each kilogram of body weight adds about 4 kg of load across the knee when walking; osteoarthritis risk rises steeply
Fatty liver disease (now the commonest liver condition), gallstones, reflux, and higher risk of bowel, liver and oesophageal cancer
Obstructive sleep apnoea and breathlessness from reduced lung volumes

guidance: Know your numbers: BMI (weight in kg divided by height in m squared; 25-30 overweight, over 30 obesity, lower cut-offs of 23 and 27.5 for South Asian, Chinese, Black African and Middle Eastern backgrounds) and waist circumference
Aim first for 5-10% loss over 3-6 months, about 0.5-1 kg a week, through a sustained energy deficit of around 600 kcal a day
Prioritise protein, vegetables and fibre; cut sugary drinks, alcohol and ultra-processed snacks; keep regular meals
Combine with 150 minutes of activity and twice-weekly strength work to protect muscle; sleep 7-9 hours
Seek structured support (group programmes, dietitian); medication or surgery are options for obesity with related disease, prescribed and monitored by specialists

smoking.name: Smoking and vaping
smoking.summary: Tobacco smoke delivers nicotine, an addictive stimulant, in a cloud of 7,000 chemicals including 70 known carcinogens, carbon monoxide and tar. It damages every organ it reaches: it is the leading preventable cause of cancer, heart disease and lung disease, and kills half of long-term users. Stopping at any age recovers much of the risk, and the fall begins within hours.
body: In the lungs, hot smoke paralyses and then destroys the cilia that sweep mucus and microbes out of the airways, inflames the bronchi (chronic bronchitis), and the enzymes released by inflammatory cells digest the walls of the alveoli (emphysema), so gas exchange fails. Tar coats the lining and its carcinogens mutate the DNA of bronchial cells: lung cancer risk is 15-30 times that of a never-smoker, and cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, bladder, pancreas, kidney, stomach, cervix and bowel are all increased.

Carbon monoxide occupies haemoglobin, cutting oxygen delivery; nicotine drives adrenaline, raising heart rate and blood pressure; and the chemicals injure the endothelium lining every artery, letting cholesterol enter the wall and making blood stickier. The result is atherosclerosis in the coronary, carotid, cerebral and leg arteries, doubling heart attack and stroke risk and causing most cases of peripheral arterial disease and aortic aneurysm.

Nicotine reaches the brain in ten seconds and releases dopamine in the reward pathway; receptors multiply, so the brain demands nicotine to feel normal and withdrawal brings irritability, restlessness and craving. That biology, not weakness, is why stopping is hard and why nicotine replacement, varenicline and behavioural support together triple the chance of success. E-cigarettes deliver nicotine without combustion and are substantially less harmful than smoking, which makes them a useful quitting tool for smokers, but they are not harmless and are not for non-smokers or young people.

effects.effect: COPD (smoking causes 9 in 10 cases), lung cancer, pneumonia, worse asthma; passive smoke causes the same diseases in others
Atherosclerosis: heart attack, stroke, aneurysm, peripheral arterial disease, erectile dysfunction
Cancers of the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, bowel; peptic ulcers; Crohn disease flares
Bladder and kidney cancer; faster decline in kidney disease
Osteoporosis, slower fracture and wound healing
Reduced fertility, miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, sudden infant death

guidance: There is no safe level of smoking; stopping completely is the goal, and the benefits start within a day (carbon monoxide gone), weeks (breathing and circulation improve), a year (heart attack risk halved) and a decade (lung cancer risk halved)
Use support: stop-smoking services, nicotine replacement (patch plus a fast-acting form), varenicline or cytisine, or switching fully to vaping
Set a quit date, remove tobacco and lighters, plan for triggers, and treat a lapse as a lesson rather than a failure
Keep homes and cars smoke-free to protect children
Smokers aged 55-74 are offered lung cancer screening with low-dose CT in a growing number of countries

alcohol.name: Alcohol
alcohol.summary: Alcohol is absorbed from the stomach and small intestine, distributed through body water and processed by the liver at roughly one unit an hour. In the short term it depresses the brain; over years it damages the liver, heart, pancreas, nerves and brain and causes seven types of cancer. Risk rises with every drink; there is no fully safe level, but keeping under 14 units a week spread over several days keeps it low.
body: The liver converts alcohol to acetaldehyde, a toxic carcinogen, and then to acetate. Fat accumulates in liver cells within days of heavy drinking (fatty liver, reversible with abstinence); continued drinking inflames the liver (alcoholic hepatitis) and scars it (cirrhosis), which blocks blood flow from the gut, backs pressure into oesophageal veins that can bleed, and destroys the liver's ability to make proteins and clear toxins.

In the brain, alcohol enhances GABA inhibition and blocks glutamate: judgement, coordination and memory fail in proportion to the blood level, and at high levels breathing and gag reflexes are suppressed, which is how binge drinking kills. Regular use makes the brain adapt, so stopping suddenly causes rebound overactivity: tremor, seizures and delirium tremens, which can be fatal without medical withdrawal. Thiamine deficiency in heavy drinkers damages the memory circuits (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome).

Alcohol raises blood pressure, causes atrial fibrillation ('holiday heart') and weakens the heart muscle (cardiomyopathy); it inflames the pancreas and the stomach lining; and acetaldehyde plus its effect on oestrogen and folate causes cancers of the mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, bowel and breast. Its calories (7 kcal per gram) contribute to weight gain, and it disrupts sleep architecture even in moderate amounts.

effects.effect: Fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis; pancreatitis; gastritis and ulcers; cancers of the mouth to bowel
Intoxication, blackouts, dependence, withdrawal seizures, peripheral neuropathy, dementia, depression
Hypertension, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, stroke
Low blood sugar in binges, raised triglycerides, gout, reduced testosterone
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder: no safe amount in pregnancy

guidance: No more than 14 units a week for both men and women, spread over 3 or more days, with several drink-free days; a unit is 10 mL of pure alcohol, roughly half a pint of ordinary beer, a small (125 mL) glass of wine, or a single 25 mL measure of spirits
Avoid binges (more than 6 units in one session); eat before drinking and alternate with water
None in pregnancy or when planning one; none before driving, operating machinery or swimming

Warning signs of dependence: needing a drink to start the day, shaking when stopping, drinking more than intended, others expressing concern; anyone drinking heavily every day should not stop abruptly without medical advice
Liver tests, blood pressure and support services (talking therapies, medication such as acamprosate or naltrexone) are available through primary care

hydration.name: Hydration
hydration.summary: Water makes up about 60% of an adult's body and is the medium for every chemical reaction, the carrier for every nutrient and waste product, and the body's coolant. The kidneys and the thirst centre match intake to loss with remarkable precision; problems arise at the extremes: dehydration in heat, illness and old age, and, more rarely, drinking so much that sodium is diluted.
body: Water leaves the body as urine (about 1.5 litres a day), sweat, water vapour in breath and a little in stool: roughly 2-2.5 litres in temperate conditions, far more in heat or exercise. About 20% of intake comes from food; the rest from drinks of any kind, since tea, coffee and milk count. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood concentration of as little as 1-2% and trigger thirst and the release of antidiuretic hormone, which tells the kidney's collecting ducts to reabsorb water and concentrate the urine.

Mild dehydration (1-2% of body weight) causes thirst, dark urine, headache, tiredness and poorer concentration; moderate dehydration lowers blood pressure, speeds the heart and reduces urine output; severe dehydration causes confusion, kidney injury and collapse. Older people feel thirst less and have less kidney reserve, babies lose water fast through their large surface area and vomiting or diarrhoea, and both need watching in hot weather and illness.

Overdrinking is the rarer danger: drinking several litres in a short time, particularly during endurance events or with some psychiatric conditions and drugs, dilutes blood sodium (hyponatraemia), swelling brain cells and causing headache, confusion, seizures and death. Sports drinks with electrolytes are needed only for sustained exercise over about an hour; for everyone else, water is the right drink, and sugary drinks are the ones to cut.

effects.effect: Adequate intake dilutes urine and halves the recurrence of kidney stones; concentrated urine irritates the bladder and favours infection
Dehydration impairs concentration, mood and reaction time and triggers headaches and migraine
Low volume drops blood pressure and causes dizziness on standing, especially with diuretics and in the elderly
Fluid keeps stool soft; constipation worsens with dehydration
Sweating is the main heat loss mechanism and fails without water; heat illness follows

guidance: Around 6-8 glasses (1.5-2 litres) of fluid a day for most adults, more in heat, exercise, fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, pregnancy and breastfeeding
Use urine colour as the guide: pale straw is right, dark yellow means drink more; thirst is a late signal in older people
Water, lower-fat milk and unsweetened tea or coffee are the best choices; limit fruit juice and smoothies to 150 mL a day and avoid sugary drinks

In illness with vomiting or diarrhoea, small frequent sips of oral rehydration solution replace salts as well as water; seek help for a baby or older person who is not passing urine, is drowsy or has sunken eyes
During prolonged exercise drink to thirst and include sodium; do not force fluids beyond that
